div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The King's Twice Married Niece.—The Grand Duchess Cyril of Russia, who has recently had a li,ttle daughter, is still quite young, having only just entered upon the thirties, but she has had rather a dramatic career. Born Princess Victoria Melita, the second daughter of the late Duke of Caxe-Coburg, she was married when only seventeen to her cousin the Grand Duke of Hesse, but that marriage was dissolved.nnd about a year ago, she became the wife of the Grand Duke Cyril. The marriage gave great offence to the Czar, and the Duke and Duchess are not received at the Russian Court, or even allowed to reside in Russia. The Grand Duchess is handsome, clever, and accomplished,a line horsewomen, and keen on all outdoor spotts. One of her most intimate friends is Miss Toupie Lowther the champion lady fencer of the world. Another German Royal Wedding.—There is to be another wedding in the German Imperial Family in May, when Prince August Wilhelm is to marry his cousin Princess Alexendra Victoi of Sonderburg-Glucks- burg. The Kaiser has six sons to provide for, none of whom, according to the Emperor's wishes, was to marry before he was twenty-one but an exception has been made in favour of`Prince,August Wilhelm, who is only nineteen, whilst his betrothed is but seventeen. The young Prince is the most studious of all the Kaiser's sons, but although more interested in the works of literature and art, he is to follow a military career, like most of his brothers. Their only sister, Princess Victoria Louise, is a girl of fifteen, of whom the Kaiser said, when she was a child, that although she often forgot he was he Emperor, she never forgot that she was the Emperor's daughter. The Romance of Gretna Green.—Some of the old registers of Gretna Green marriages, are supposed to be in America, but mostly all traces of these records have been lost, and the proposal that they should be collected, seems to be rather a hopeless one. It is just fifty years since Gretna Green ceased to be the Mecca of runaway couples, owing to the Act which made a three week's residence in Scotland necessary. That Act was influenced to a great extent by the Earl of Jersey's family, owing to the runaway marriage of Lady Adele Villiers, with Captain Ibbetson. In the old -days, elopements were a not uncommon event in nearly every great family. Lady Adele Villiers' grandmother, the daughter of Mr. Child, the Londen banker, was married to Lord Westmorland at Gretna Green. but social manners changed, and the old-fashioned elope- ments came to be regarded as more of a scandal thrip as material for romance. They are quite out of date nowadays, and one of the last of the Society runaway matches was that of the Marchioness of Hastings who died the ott-er day. Whilst engaged to Mr. Henry ftChaplin, she eloped with the Marquis of Hastings, and 'after his death four years later, she married the late George Chetwynd. Marrying the Voter.—One of the present Cabinet Ministers when pressed on the question of Women's Suffrage, evaded a direct answer, by saying that he thought every woman ought to have a vote, or a voter. Miss Teresa Billington, one of the strenuous suffragists, appears to have been of the same opinion, for having delared that she would never Marry until women had votes, she changed her mind, and was last week quietly married to Mr. F. L. Greig, at Glasgow. One notices that she signs herself Billington-Greig, which suggests that she does not intend to efface her identity. it suffragist she was, and a suffragist she remains and pre- sumably Mr. Greig is going to help carry the banner on to victory. Servants' Compensation.—The uncertainty' which attaches to the responsibility of householders under the new Compensation Act, must rejoice the hearts of the lawyers, who together with the Insurance Companies seem likely to obtain most of the benefit from this new departure in domestic legislation. One of the most likely pitfalls for the householder relates to the , employment of the extra woman for the spring cleaning I or the odd man or gardener, and there is little doubt that the Act will prove exceedingly injurious to those who depend upon casual employment, such as char- women and others, seeing that many people will refrain from calling in their aid. Moreover the householder I who insures cannot be sure of entire freedom from liability. All the Insurance Companies require that i notice of accident must be given within a few days, but supposing Mary Jane trips over a mat and thinks nothing of it until a week later when she complains of some internal injury. Such, and many other contin- gencies appear to await the householder,even under the protection of an insurance policy. Croquet.—Of late years croquet has regained much of its old favour, and all appearances point to its being very popular this summer. It is of course, early yet to be thinking about outdoor recreations, but with Easter not far ahead, we shall soon be looking forward to our favourite lawn games. Only a few years ago, croquet usedto be satirised as feeble and effeminate, but it has come to recognized that as now played, there is a great of skill and science in the game, and the fact that it is not so strenuous as lawn tennis is all in its favour for women and girl players. It was a Miss acnau ghten —the daughter of Sir Richard Macnaughten who revived the moClern era of the game in Ireland, and who was also the means of introducing it into England by first playing the Castle. That was in If3;:'\e on the lawns at Lowther was living, and after that i 7 when the late Lord Lonsdalo ing its public favour of manspread like wildfire, retain-. y years, before lawn tennis challenged its popularity. • Glove Stretchers and Boot Tr e like boot trees, are a necessity to the Glove stretchers woman who would appear well-dressed. And now-a CI both are quite , within the reach of the girl or ;nay% who has but a should be made moderate dress allowance. No attempt to put on %nee pair of gloves withoift fl'rhs stretchers to loosen the tips,and shaking a first us into the fingers, and all gloves in wear sthiitilda be gone over with the stretchers from time to them well into the tips, a procedure that will help the regard to to retain their shape to the last. With to boot trees, many new and wonderful devices have gard consisting found their way into the market, of lattaYea te doubtful whether the old wooden varietih,s, rnit is of three pieces, have ever been improved ufton. A range of sizes is stocked in all the large ernporiurnswan it is almost always possible to secure the one desired. At sale times these particular trees are often priced as low as two shillings, and the benefit in appearance ands wear, to boots that soend the greater part of their time upon them is marvellous. Bargains at the White Sales.—The White Sales are now in full swine, and veritable bargains in the way of lawn, linen, muslin and lace gowns, are to be found

therein. There is very little risk attached to these purchases, as the majority, when made, are furnished with sleeves that will pass muster this year, unmade, which being translated means that a length of material is provided for the bodice, and that the skirt has to be joined up the back, fixed into a waistband—there is only the cut of the skirt to take into consideration. In nearly all instances however, the skirts fit closely about the hips, and flow out well, below the knees, a mode likely to be approved in high quarters this spring and coming summer. About Umbrellas.—Many umbrellas, and en-tout-cas, are being filled with receptacles in the handle, for pins, or the tiny puff so many women find indispensable. This means that the knob is in favour again, though when pins only are required, other shapes are possible. Another attempt has been made to push forward brightly hued silk umbrellas, but so far we will have none of them, and remain faithful to black, dark brown and what is known as invisible green. MADG E.

"And what name shall I say, sir ? " "Will you just say a gentleman to see her, Dad following this announcement he entemi a room as perfect in its way as it could be, witu the sunlight streaming into it, and bright flowers in the window-boxes, and flowers in vases every- where. The woman who rose to receive him looked curiously at him as the door closed. "You have hardly changed at all in looks," said Thurstan, quietly. "Is it really you?" she said. "Mildred! .

"I have been expecting you," she said, nestling ato the arms held out to her, "but I was almost afraid to hope. Five years is a long time. "And it has been hard for you," he answered. "I have been to the Gables."

"Have you seen your uncle ? " "No, he refuses to see me; but tell me all the story. What did you quarrel with him about ? " "The quarrel was altogether on one side," she answered. "For a few months after you had gone everything went on as usual, except that Mr. Chexfield shut himself up more. Sometimes did not see him for three or four days together? and he took to sending me little scraps of notes to Lay that he was too busy reading to go out, or that he had a headache. You can understand that I was a little depressed without you - Jack, and as I was invited to spend a fevi weeks with some old schoolfellows in Cornwall, Mr. Chex- field suggested that I should go. I saw him for a few minutes on the morning I left, and he was just the same as usual. When I came back, it was rather late in the.evening ; he had gone to bed, but he left a note for me with Mrs. Harper, welcoming me home. Two days after he sent me another note saying that he expected a gentleman to call and see me, and that he wished me to approve of this gentleman's suggestion. I thought that he had relented and sent for you, and you cannot know how impatiently I waited. The gentleman came the next day, a perfect stranger to me, and made me an offer of. marriage. It was my guardian's wish he said, and was for my benefit. He laid the matter before me like some business scheme for my approval. I should have done better perhaps to temporise, but I did not. I indignantly refused the offer, and tried to obtain an interview with Mr. Chexfield. It was no use. He would not see me, and never has seen me since. He wrote me -a note telling me either to obey, or leave the house, and I left the house. It appears that I had a little money of riy own; at any rate, Mr. Chextield paid me two thousand pounds, and I hay.e lived here with Mrs. Burt ever since. I could not go away from Way- lands because of you, and besides-" _

_ "And what besides ? " "I should like to see Mr. Chexfield again. "After he has treated you so badly ? " "There may be a reason, Jack. You see, ho is treating you in much the same way." "Who was this man ? "
"A Mr. Foster. Poor man, he has wasted a terrible lot of time over me. He has been most persistent, and is constantly at the Gables." "Staying there do you mean ? " Thurstan asked. "Yes." _ _ _

"Foster? Foster? I never heard the name. Perhaps I shall see him if he is there now, for I intend to stay a few days. That annoyance will soon be ended at any rate, dearest, and I am thankful to say we canido without my uncle." "You have prospered ? " "Prospered ! " he exclaimed, with the happy laugh of a man who has won in life's race, and sitting with his arm round her he told her the history of that five years. It was just eight o'clock when Thurstan got back to the Gables, and Mr. Harper opened the door for him. There was almost a welcome in .her tone as 'she led him into the small room again where supper was laid, and for one only he noticed. _ _ _

"I hear that you constantly have a visitor here, Mrs. Harper." "Ah ! don't talk of him, sir," she exclaimed. "Yes, he is here now, but has not come in yet. I have thought he may have been the cause of the quarrel with Miss Rickard." "It is possible," said Thurstan, indifferently. He was not inclined to speak too freely to Mrs. Harper, for she may have had something to do with turning his uncle against Mildred, and perhaps against himself too. "Of course, it's no business of mine," said Mrs. Harper, and left the room. Thurstan sat down to his lonely supper, a happy smile upon his face. If his uncle did not want to see him, what did it really matter? Mildred had not changed, and that was every- thing. It was an exceedingly pleasant reverie in which he lost himself. Suddenly he started. A door in a distant passage opened and there was the sound of shuffling feet. "Go to bed," said Mrs. Harper's sharp voice. "Why shouldn't I see him ? " questioned a stammering voice. "He's my rival, don't you know. 'Spect we should get along excellently together." "The mysterious Foster," said Thurstan, going to the door; "and the mysterious Foster has been drinking, I fancy." As he went into the hall Mrs. Harper was saying: "Go gently, sir, do, or you will wake the master." _ _ .

"Good thing, too! Do him good to be roused up a bit. , Ah, there you are! How do, rival. Shall I come and keep you company ? " He turned as if to come down tho few steps which Mr. and Mrs. Harper had succeeded in getting him to mount. "Not to-night," Thurston answered. going to bed directly." "Shall I come and have a yarn in your room ? " "Leave it until to-morrow." "All right. 'Spect we'll be grand pals in spite cf the girl, eh ? " "Perhaps so," answered Thurston, as he went back into the room, and the thought of this brute daring to annoy Mildred made him mutter an oath underneath his breath.
"I am
Presently Mrs. Harper came to him. "Is he often like that ? " Thurstan inquired. "Sometimes," and there was an angry flash in

. , the woman's oyes. ' "And he has taken my place with my uncle. What does it matter? Mildred is the same." He spoke to himself rather than to Mrs. Harper, and she made no answer as she cleared the supper away. "I shall go to be& Where am I to sleep, Mrs. Harper ? " "I will shew you," she answered. "Mr. Foster has the room you used to occupy. I have prepared the long bedroom for yqu by the master's orders." ".I am an honoured guest, it seems, although he will not see me." • Mrs. Harper led the way up the wide staircase, and along two or three passages. At the end of one of these was a green baize door which shut off the rooms occupied by Mr. Chexfield, and at the end of another was the long bedroom. It had evidently been built as the chief guest-chamber, and although somewhat sparsely furnished for so large a room, was comfortable enough. Mrs. Harper lit two candles standing on a table near the bed, and drew up a deep easy-chair to the table. "I hope you will sleep well," she said, and left him. _ _

..... It was not the first time Thurstan had been in this room, but he had never slept in it, nor did he remember to have been in it except in day- light. It looked eerie in the meagre light of the two candles, and was full or strange, distorted shadOws. Moonlight shone through the two long windows, and fell in two broad bands across the floor. div.head: WOMAN'S REALM.
div.p: WOMAN'S REALM.
DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
SHOES FOR EVENING WEAR

For evening wear shoes of silver tissue havi entirely ousted those of black kid, or, indeed, of any other kind, even the examples designed in gold tissue being but rarely seen nowadays. The toes of the shoes are extraordinarily long and pointed, while for afternoon wear • black shoes. cut in the Louis XIII. style, are high in favour, the buckles being of jet cat square and of enormous size. Coloured shoes, which were recently so much worn with black toilets, have been almost completely abandoned in this con- nection. an exception being. however, the grey suede boot with patent leather golosh.

div.head: CLOTH CAPELETS
div.p: CLOTH CAPELETS

Little cloth capes are being tnide to match the new cloth gowns for spring • wear. These fascinating garments are cut with long pointed ends in front, and are . slit up -to form square epaulettes over the shoulders and a square piece behind. The spaces between the epaulettes are bridged over with a lattice-work of velvet ribbon, the whole of the cape beimg bordered with a bouillonneo of satin to mach the colour of the cloth.
GREEN SERGE COAT,

A spring coat for a small girl has been chosen for the theme of our illustration. It is intended to be realised in a pretty shade Of green serge, a colour that seems most in keeping with the early spring season. The coat is made like a tunic. with three box-pleats down back and front, held

in by a narrow strap-belt placed round the hips. The sleeves are laid in tucks as they near the wrist, and are finished with a little . turn-back velvet cuff embroidered, in various shades cif green. A double cape lies over the shoulders, passing beneath the central box-pleat back and front. The under one is of serge, the upper one of velvet, embroidered round the edge with the same design as that used on the cuffs. A velvet hat, with flop brim and Tam-o'-Shanter crown, worn with this little coat, trimmed with two large soft silk rosettes, one above and one be- neath the brim. , FASHIONS IN MILLINERY.

Now is the time when we begin to think that are long we shall be choosing our spring mil- linery with great enjoyment; but at present, says the Queen, there is very little sign of any break in the winter. Those bound for the South have a good deal of dainty millinery provided for them. Large velvet hats and any -amount of feathers of pretty well every kind are provided for the votaries of fashion. Women who have large faces do not look well in a small hat, and that is why just now a good deal of the .millinery looks so singularly unbecoming, and uniess the hats and toques are arranged just at the right an!-:•le they have anything but a good appearance. Placing them backwards or forwards makes all the difference in their becomingness. and some- times the introduction of another bow or another wing 'will transform the whole thing. Black hats are not so modish as those that match the toilet, and yet more black is worn than anything else, and sometimes the effect of the dress is spoilt thereby; but, still, there are 'very few colours that black does mot go well with. There are quite as many stiff shapes as there are soft shapes, but as a rule the soft are the more be- coming, especially where the face is young and fresh. The stiff shapes have crowns of medium height, generally surrounded by a fold of mate- rial, and bands of satin or velvet border Many of 1 the brims. Tulle and velvet mingle, and nothing I is so fashionable as ostrich plumes • however stiff ! and hard the hat may be, it is softened by their ! introduction.

div.head: VIYELLA SHIRT BLOUSE.
div.p: VIYELLA SHIRT BLOUSE.

The plain shirt blouse for morning wear al- ways holds its own, and, except in the details of trimming, they vary very little from season to season. The main point is to be certain that tho pattern from which they are cut is a good one and fits the intended wearer. The best plan is to buy one really good plain shirt, and when worn out unpick it and use it as a guide for future generations of blouses. Our illustration. shews a plain viyella shirt blouse having two in- verted box-pleats over each shoulder: and an

open space in the central front which is filled in with a strip of fancy tucked material; or, if the same flannel is used, it should be embroidered along each tuck. Smart little white linen collars and cuffs worked with French knots in coloured silk give a pretty finish; and a wide elastic belt, such as can now be obtained in almost any shade, finishes off the blouse Neatly at the waist. THE SHORT DANCING FROCK.

1 The short dancing frock has really arrived, says a Globe writer. Ball-rooms now present a much more graceful appearance, since the girls can hold themselves straight, and their gar ments flow out without restraint. There are real I dangers about a long skirt unless it is held I well up out of the way. In the, backward steps ; of the two-step or the waltz, to tread on ones .own skirt while going at such a pace as is now the fashion may result in a very nasty fall on the back of the head. We saw a lady meet with such an accident at one dance, and it was ren- -1 demi seriou by the fact that she was wearing : a high, carved comb, the teeth of which entered 1 her head and made a wound which was long in healing. Even on less tragic occasions the skirt : conies in for a great deal of damage.

div.head: TO-DAY'S RECIPE
div.p: TO-DAY'S RECIPE

MULLIGATAWNY SOUP.—Slice one large Spanish onion, and fry a golden brown in 2oz. of butter; add three tablespoonfuls of curry powder or paste, 'stir in gradually half a pint of stock, then add one tablespoonful of currant jelly, the juice of half a lemon, and one dessertspoonful of chut- ney; mix well, add three pints of stock, and leave it to simmer half-an-hour. Now pulp all through a wire sieve, melt 2oz. of butter, add 2oz. of flour, keep stirring all .the time, and gradually add the soup; stir till it boils. Just before serv- . MP' nut in a. litt cream. Rabbits make excel- lent stock for mulligatawny soup. Instead of the cream, a little of the white meat may be pounded and served in it. Boiled rice to be handed with the soup.

div.head: 'AIYSTERY OF THE GABLES.
div.p: THE 'AIYSTERY OF THE GABLES.
DY CHRISTIAN LYS,
Author of "The Fortress of Yada,sare,," "The Hepsworth Millions," "The Mystery of Lady- place," "The Doctor's Idol," &c.

There appeared to be no reason why the rail- way company had built a station at that par- ticular spot. Wayland's and Morth it was called, and it may have been anticipated that the neigh- bourhood would develop in time, Which it never had done, and consequently only about two trains in the day stopped there. As it seldom happened that anyone was waiting to get into them, or that anybody wanted to get out, this was more a matter of form than anything else. This afternoon, however, a single passenger ighted carrying a bag. The solitary porter iooked at him as he took his ticket, wondering what he had come for, and fully expected to be asked the way to somewhere; but the stranger passed out and went down the road in the direc- tion of Waylands, a village about three miles away, as though he were quite familiar with the neighbourhood. _

There are probably few people beyond those who have been born there who really know this part of the coniktry lying in the heart of Blank- shire. The stream of life and progress which flows on all sides does not penetrate into it, the traveller has no busineSs there, and although the railway company made a feeble attempt to open it up by building a station and commenting upon its beauties in the railway guide, hardly a straugef beyond an occasional artist ever enters it. The scenery is wild in its way, and the district is noted for the number of old houses in it, houses which have sadly fallen away from their former grandeur and which are, in many oases, either crumbling into ruins, or have been bolstered up to serve as barns and stables. That the man walked briskly pointed him out as a stranger at once, for no native ever got beyond a sleepy pace which had no consideration of time in it; and he .did not look like an artist. At the top of a hill he paused to rest for a moment. In a hollow below him lay the village, a few curling wreaths of smoke above it alone _hewing that it was not deserted, And to the right the many gables of a large house were visible through the trees. "Just the Same," said the man aloud. "I wonder whether the people, all the people, are the same too ? "

He picked up his bag, which he tad dropped by the roadside, and went on. Before reaching the village he turned from the main road into a narrow lane which ran at right angles to it. Grass had sprung up in the rutty roadway, and no one had taken the trouble to cut back the hedges which straggled across as though to meet each other, and close up the right of way altogether. A quarter of a mile down the lane, which there ended, stood the house with the many gables, a large, picturesque place, green with moss and lichen, which .flourished in every crevice, and surrounded by a garden which had grown wild and desolate from neglect. "This looks as though he had become more eccentric than ever," mused the man as he pushed open the rusty gate. "I wonder whether Mildred still keeps her little patch of garden bright." He went to the front door and pulled a crazy- looking bell, but before he was sure whether it had rung or not, the door was opened a little way, and a tall, powerful-looking woman con- fronted him. She had a hard, set face, and grizzly black and grey hair, and she eyed the stranger with evident distrust, ready to slam the door in his face at a moment's notice. At any rate she had not changed very much, the man thought. "Is Mr. Chexfield in ? " "He is."
"Can I see him ? " "Most unlikely. What's your business ?" "You do not remember me, Mrs. Harper ? " The woman bent forward to look more critically into his face.

"No, and yet--.." "Ah, I thought a beard could not have altered me out of all recognition." "Are you John Thurstan ? " she asked. "I am, and I have come to keep my appoint- ment with my ur -le, five years to the day. "Didn't know you had any appointment, and I'm not at all sure of your identity, and I don't suppose for a moment that Mr. Chexfield will see you, but you may come in. Mr. Chexfield has changed a good bit in five years." Thurstan followed her across the hall into a small room, a room he remembered extremely well. It was here he had parted from his uncle.

"I'll tell Mr. Chexfield," said Mrs. Harper. She went out, closing the door after her, and Thurstan walked to the NNindow. It looked on to the spacious gardens at the back of the house, which were just such another waste as those in front. Five years ago there had been a bright patch in it which Mildred had tended, but even this was gone, nothing but weeds and rank grass there now. Had Mildred changed too ? It seemed a short time to look back over, and be saw himself in a truer light than he had done then. Although eccentric, his uncle had been kind to him. He had stayed at the house when he liked, his intercourse with his uncle's ward, Mildred Rickard, the only daughter of a very old friend who had died in poor circumstances, had been unchecked, and he had Supposed that, as he was the only relative his uncle had, he would in due time come into his money, a very considerable fortune according to common retort. The awakening ,had come suddenly and unexpectedly on the very day that Mildred had promised to marry .him. "My dear John," Mr. Chexfield had said, "I am not going to put Mildred into the hands of a man who ha's no settled purpose in life, who has wasted his early years in the expectation of inheriting money, and looks forward to spending the remainder of them in luxurious idleness. There is a hundred pounds. Go into the world and use it, hold no communi- cation with Mildred for five years, and then come back. I make the appointment now, and for every hundred you have made I will give you a hundred, and we can talk about Mildred then. She is young, the waiting will not hurt her, and it will give her time to know her own mind." So John. Thurstan hrkl gone and had turned to ard work abroad. If Mr. gone, kept to his part .of the bargain his fortune was destined to suffer considerable reduction.

Nearly half-an-hour elapsed before Mrs. Harper returned. "It is as I thought," she said. "Mr. Chexfield will not sec you." - "Not see me ? " Thurston exclaimed. "I told you he had changed," she said, in a more 'conciliatory ,tone. "He seldom goes out now, hardly ever leaves his rooms, in fact, and sits over his books and papers as though life held nothing else. He says you are welcome to stay here if you like." "Very good of him." "Humour him and stay, Mr. Thurston." "You think he will see me presently?" "Can't say." • She watched him as he paced up and , down considering. "Where is Miss Rickard ? "he asked suddenly. "She does not attend to the garden as she used to do." "She isn't here to do it; hasn't been here for nearly four years. She and Mr. Chexfield quarrelled, and the, master turned her out of the house. She is living in the village." "What did they quarrel about ? " "I don't know." .

"i will -stay, Mrs. Harper," Thurstan said. "I will walk into the village and see Miss,. Zliekard. " "And you'll be back by eight ? " said Mrs. Harper. "We shut up the house at that time now. Master's orders. I'll have some supper waiting for you.. it's the house next the church where Miss Rickard lives." An old man was in the garden as he went out, half dozing over his pipe. "Still in the land of the living, Harper ?" "Yes, sir, still here. So the master won't see you ? " "Not yet." "Are you coming back?" "Yes. Harper said nothing but gave a groan, whether of satisfaction or not it was impossible to tell. The pleasant-looking old lady who opened the _door to Thurstan informed him that Miss Rickard was at home.

bect-VrMi-length portrait or-a wonian sthndiiig erect. Abormally tall the black-robed figure looked, and the flesh-colour had not grown dull with time. The picture may have 'caught some reflected moonlight, but at any rate the figuie seemed to stand out from the surrounding gloom, and the eyes stared fixedly at the bed. Thurstan. •could not help thinking .that a nervous person might well be preven.ped from sleeping soundly with those eyes fixed upon him all night. He took a newspaper from his bag and made himself comfortable in the armchair. He was met used to such early hours. The candles burnt steadily, and he read paragraph after paragraph, not much interested, but yet not sleepy. He read mechanically, hardly conscious of what he read, and presently fancied himself with Mildred, and that Foster was with them, and that Mildred turned from him to Foster, and then—the nodding of his head, aroused him; the paper was lying on the floor and the candles were per- ceptibly shorter. • must have dropped off," he said, picking up the paper and looking at his watch. it was past midnight, and the bands of moonlight on the floor had travelled nearer to the portrait. It was strange how the eyes seemed to look at him, he had only noticed that they stared at the bed before. The light seemed to catch them in a curious way, and to give them life. They seemed to close for an instant, and then to watch him more intently than ever. He took up a candle and crossed the room to look at the portrait more closely. The eyes were fixed upon the bed, no real life in them. They 'were, indeed', not a good specimen of the painter's art. "A trick of moonlight makes me fanciful," he said. "It is well that I am not a nervous person." He opened one of the windows softly. It was a still night, not a breath stirring, not a rustle in the wilderness of a garden below him. A creeper, tough and strong with age, climbed to the window, and the branches of a tree there would have tapped ghost-like on the panes had there been a breeze to move them. The utter silence without and within 'was not enough to make him nervous, but his imagination began to run riot. Did his uncle sit reading far into the night? Why did he never come out of those rooms? Why would he not see him ? And crowding upon such questions came others, bring- ing with them answers which seemed absurd. "And yet--" he paused and closed the window gently. A problem had presented itself ; ,to his mind, and he said in a whisper, "I'll find 1 out."

He did not light the candles. He went to ?iicdeuncoets. object to the renewal of any of the existing the bed to turn back the clothes and started The Chairman said they might consider the report on back with a low cry. The bed was already the whole satisfactory. occupied. A man lay there asleep, sound asleep. All the existing licences were renewed. Thurstan's touch had not roused him. Could I THE CT AND LION, STRETTON. Foster have come to his room after all ? He lit Mr. Browne, solicitor, Warrington, applied for the a candle and held it up to look. It was Foster, ! transfer of the licence of the Cat and Lion, Stretton, asleep, dead asleep. The next instant Thurstan from Joseph Broady to Robert Walker, who, he said, grasped the flame in his hand to extinguish it. had kept the Talbot Hotel, Sankey-street, Warrington, years. Darkness was safer, for the light had shewn .the for seven • ication was granted. man not asleep, but dead, and the handle of a The application thin long knife which was pinned through the bedclothes into his heart. Thurstan turned and, as it were, felt the room with his eyes. The murderer was not there he was convinced, but he would return. Thurstan replaced the bed- clothes hurriedly, and stood back in the folds of the curtains of the bed and waited. Had that fatal knife been intended for him? He could not doubt it. And it was by his uncle'sl orders he had been put in that room; the fact insisted on being remembered. Should he escape at once, or had the lighted candle already betrayed him to some watcher? He waited, listening ' and counting his chances. Suddenly he remem- bered the creeper at the window, There lay.his way of escape. - He had made one step from the folds of the curtains when he drew back. There was a slight grating noise in the room, and he saw the portrait draw back, and from where it had been, two figures stepped quietly into the room. "Have yca left him long enough? Is he dead ? "

"Did you ever know me anything else but thorough ? " was the answer. It was Mrs. Harper. She came quickly towards the bed. "Hide the face," whispered her husband. "I cannot bear to look upon a dead face." The woman appeared to have no desire to look upon her victim either. She twisted the clothes round the dead man, and together, by the head and feet, she and her husband carried him across the room. There were a few whispered words which Thursta,n could not catch, and then the portrait was there again. Five minutes later Thurstan had lowered himself to the ground by the creeper, having closed the window after him. The hours seemed long waiting for the village to awake, and when he found the constable he had great difficulty in getting him to believe his story. . .

_ —"lf what you say is true, it's' a bigger business than you imagine. We must he careful, and get help.' So it happened that when, just after eight o'clock, Thurstan went up to the front door and rang the crazy bell, a score of willing helpers were hidden about the gardens and in the lane. Some time elapsed before the bolts were drawn. Then the door opened slowly. "Is Mr. Chexfield in ? " For one moment the woman stared itt him, and then with a cry she threw up her arms and laughed until the old house echoed agaiil? Her husband came hurriedly across the hall to her, but he stopped short upon seing .Thurstan, and stood as if turned to stone, uttering not a word.

I Frank Pitta tramp. walked up to a policemen at St. Austell and said : "Do you want a job ? I have stolen this waistcoat from a shop door, and I want to be locked up." At the St. Anstell Police Court he was sentenced to one month's imprisonment.

It was impossible to say precisely how long ; Mr. Chextield had been dead, but most probably be was murdered during Miss Rickard's stay in Cornwall, as it was about this time that the realisation of his property had commenced, and a large amount of the money was found in the house. It appeared that Mr. Chatfield had invested a considerable sum in the names of trustees for Mildred Rickard, and no doubt this was why Mrs. Harper conceived the idea of marrying her to her son, Arthur Foster Harper. That the son was innocent of much of his mother's villainy seemed certain from the manner and place of his death. No doubt his drunken humour had prompted him to go and Pak to Thurstan' and finding the room empty, he had thought it a good joke to get into his bed, there to fall asleep never to wake again. His body, still wrapped in the bedclothes, was found in a pit in the passage behind the portrait, and Mr. Chexfield's remains were also discovered there, lightly covered with earth. Earth would probably have been thrown in upon Foster 's body in due course. Doubtless Mrs. Harper would have ultimately left Waylands, but her success and greed caused her to remain until the last penuy possible had been obtained, and she had only parted with two thousand pounds to Miss Rickard as a safeguard against inconvenient inquiries being made at the Gables. The sudden return of John Thurstan placed her in imminent danger, for unless he was promptly got rid of, he would sooner or later force his wav to his uncle, and so lead to discovery. She had therefore, used her knowledge. of the old priest- hole, with its watching-place through the eyes of the portrait, and had succeeded in murdering the occupant of the bed—her son.

Many Points, however, remained unsolved, and are likely to remain so, for the guilty woman became a raving maniac at the sight of Thurstan, and her husband, possibly little more than a tool in her bands, strangled himself in his cell with a strip of his clothing before the day of his trial.
That Mildred Thurstan and her lrlsband have never been to Waylands since their marriage is hardly to be wondered at.
[THE ENr.]

div.head: LIBERALISM IN STOCKTON HEATH
div.p: LIBERALISM IN STOCKTON HEATH
Annual Meeting of the Association.

The annual meetinf, of the Stockton Heath Liberal Association was held on Monday evening in Providence Schoolroom, Chapel-lane, Mr. H. Roberts presiding over a small attendance. Letters of apology for non atten- ance were read for Mr. J. Longland and the Rev. J. S. Hughes.

Mr. E. LLOYD-JONES, hon. secretary, in his report, stated that they had not had many meetings since the last general Council owing partly to want of funds. That difficulty had now been overcome, and the Treasurer's statement would show-that they were on a firm footing. The registration was attended to during the year, and they came out very satisfactorily. As regarded their present position, the officers felt that they were ready to go forward. They ought to have more meetings of an educational character. There were plenty of young men in Stockton Heath, and if they were to invite the members of the Warrington junior Liberal Association to take part in a meeting he thought it would have a good effect. They ought to bring the burning questions of the day before the people, so that when the time came to secure again the return of Mr. King to Parliament they would be ready. Mr. J. Battersby, hon. treasurer, presented the balance sheet. He said a deficit had been wiped out by a donation of £3 3s. from their President, and they had a small balance in hand at the close of the year. The President said be agreed with the Secretary that they must do something more of an educational char- acter, and with that object he should be glad to increase his subscription for this year to £5. (Applause.) The suggestion to invite the Warrington Junior Liberals was also a good one. He had a high opinion of political debating societies, but the difficulty used to be that they were all on one side and it was not always easy to gat serious opposition from the conservative side. He thought they must have a series of public meetings to instruct the members, as there was no doubt that Stockton Heath, which was rapidly growing, was going to play an important part in the future of the Knutsford division. Mr. W. H. Sherburn moved the adoption of the balance sheet.
Asked to second the motion Mr. Garside declined on the ground that he was slightly interested in the aecounts.
The President : I don't mind if you are. This is not a non-trading society. (Laughter.) Mr. W. Grounds seconded, and the balance sheet was adopted.
ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

The following officers were re-elected :—President, Mr. H. Roberts, on the proposition of Mr. E. Lloyd. Jones seconded by Mr. J. W. Brayshaw ; vice-president, Mr. J. Longland, on the propositien of Mr. Jones, seconded by Mr. E. Vernon ; chairman of committee, Mr. W. H. Sherbern, .on the proposition of Mr. Battersby, seconded by Mr. Vernon ; hon. treasurer, Mr. Battersby, on the proposition of Mr. Braysbaw, seconded by Mr. Garside, and supported by Mr. Sher. burn ; hon. secretary, Mr. E. Lloyd-Jones, and assistant hon. secretary, Mr. Grounds, on the motion of the President, seconded by Mr. J. Bayne. The following were elected members of the Execu- tive Committee :—Rev. J. S. Hughes, Messrs. J. Speak- man, S. Albinson, T. Miller, H. Law,.Drewett, Hyde, Brayshaw, Lowe, Brindley, Garside, R. B. Wood, S. Gerrard, Roughsedge, 3. Richmond, E. Vernon, H. Brown, J. ging, J. Bayne, George Whitfield, H. G. Roberts, and P. Shelburn. On the proposition of Mr. W. H. Sherburn, seconded by Mr. Brayshaw, it was decided to hold quarterly meetings of the Executive Committee.
The o-iticials were instructed to a programme of periodical debates to commence forthwith.

AMONG THE CANNIBALS.

"There is much of the New Hebrides still utterly unknown," says a contributor to the" Windsor " ; "and the antiquarian and ethnological problems suggested at every turn are enough to madden any luckless traveller who, like myself, has just enough knowledge to perceive the existence of countless mysteries, and not enough to unravel any of them. No white man's foot has ever crossed Malekula (Mallicolo), the second largest, and much the most dangerous, of the New Hebrides. Only a belt round the coast and parts of the southern half is known. A truct of dense bush in the interior, about thirty by seventy miles, is peopled by savages ; who, in many cases, have never been down to the coast, and never seen the face of a white I man. The bush-tracks are almost impossible to ! traverse without a guide' and the natives are so' ! murderous and cunning that an armed force would be necessary to any exploring party who might try to make a way through. Rifles, poisoned arrows, and poisoned spearheads artfully buried in loose ground to pierce the stranger's foot are among their weapons of defence. Their villages are surrounded by labyrinthine paths intended to battle intruders ; and, like the Royal Irish Constabulary on a certain historic occasion, they don't hesitate to shoot' if any one succeeds in finding the town."—From an interesting article on "The Cannibal New Hebrides," which appears in the February "Wiudsor Magazine,"a remarkably varied and attractive number, containing complete stories by Robert Barr, Barry Pain, lan MacLaren, and other clever novelists, in Addition to a large instalment of Max Pemberton's absorbing new romance "The Lodestar." No fewer than twenty-eight cartoons of leading men of letters are admirably reproduced in colour, and some twenty-two pictures of that accomplished young artist, Mr. Harold Speed, form an interesting fine art section.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, FIAGAZEES
div.p: NEW BOOKS, FIAGAZEES
ETC.
" Andrew Goodfellow," by Mrs. Herbert Watson. Macmillan and Co., G. -

With "Andrew Goodfellow," a tale of 1805, Mrs. Herbert Watson makes her first appearance as a novelist. The book is semi-histolical, and gives passing glimpses of the notable people of the time, bat its chief charm is in the delightful characters of the Little Lieutenant," Andrew Goodfellow, and the gentle but spirited heroine, Dorothy Love!. The scenes are chiefly laid in Plymouth, and there is a real breath of the sea through the pages of the book. The story is charmingly written —wholesome and hearty in every page. One can have nothing but praise for Mrs. Watson's clever character- isation. In Andrew Goodfellow she has created a hero whom all mast love and admire. We have just one complaint. The title of the book is too colourless and unromantic. "The Little Lieutenant" should have been on the cover and title-page. Many people might reasonably imagine that "Andrew Goodfellow" stood for the biography of some uninteresting person they had never heard of, instead of for one of the most artistically-written romances of the year. "Her Majesty's Rebels," by Sidney Lysaght Macmillan and Co., Os. Mr. Lysaght is one of those writers who can com- bine love and polittcs in the pages of fiction with a master hand. In his new novel "Her Majesty's RAels " the tangled skein ofallove and politics is cleverly and dramatically unravelled. It is a power- ful story, with much that is fresh and orioDnival in it, and holds the attention of the reader from beginning to end. The author has been especially successful in , his treatment of Irish character. High and row, gentry and 'peasantry are drawn with a sure toucli,and with genuine sympathy and appreciation. Indeed we r doubt whether a truer picture of Ireland during the last century, with its discontented people clamouring for Home Rule, and grumbling at' the " rint " has been draw, a by either novelist or historian. The central dominating figure of the story—a young Irish Catholic who leads the political revolt—bears such a resemblance in many ways to Parnell that the author warns us against imagining there was any intention of bringing the great Irish agitator and Parliamentarian into the story. Michael Desmond, however, is a sufficiently interesting personality quite apart from this, and the same may be said of his brother, Connor Desmond, the real hero. Politics do not fill the book by any means. There is a strong human interest throughout, and the lives and pharac- ters which become familiar to us as we read. possess Vie fascination which a clever writer perfectly in tune with his work can alone impart. ". Her Majesty's Ret 31s "is far above the ordinary level of fiction, and in many ways is a really strong story. We can heartily recommend it to readers of both sexes who like light literature which has not the fault of being too light and transparent.
"Who's Who," by Messrs. A. and C. Black,

Messrs. A. and C. Black have just issued the new volume of " Who's Who" and the " Who's Who Year Book for 1907." " Who's Who" this year contains over 21,000 biographies, every one of which has been submitted for personal revision. It is invaluable both as a directory and as a compendium of useful facts. It is published in two styles of binding —in red cloth at 10a. net and in full limp leather at 125.6 d. net. "Who's Who Year Book "(is. net) comprises the various tables that once formed part of " Who's Who "itself. It is most useful as a reference book, as it includes not only the gist of the information con- tained in many expensive publications, but some original tables to be found nowhere else. "The Englishwoman's Year Book" has also been issued by Messrs. Black. This is the 27th edition and should therefore need very little introduction to the "public woman." The volume includes new articles by Mrs. Henry Fawcett,L.L. D. on "Women's Suffrage," by the Rev. Cecil Grant on by "Co-Educa- tion " by Miss Hotine on " Civil Service." Miss Nixon on Domestic Service. The volume is one of over 400 pages and is replete with information of every kind that women may reasonably inquire about. The sections include Education, Employment and and Professions, Industrial, Medicine. Pharmacy and Dentistry, Science, Literature, trt, Music, Sports and Pastimes, Philanthropy, Temperance, Homes and societies, Religious Work, Events of the year, Ooituary and Directory. Riches and Poverty," by L. G. Chiozza Money; Methuen and C 0.,,

A third edition of the above has just been issued by Messrs. Methuen. The volume is for several reasons of special interest at this time. It contains the remarkable evidence which Air. Chiozza-Money placed before the Income Tax Committee, including ttte facts ag to the distribution of wealth in the United Kingdom quoted by Sir Henry Primrose before the same Committee, and the suggestions as to the form of a graduated scale. The book was so much dis- cussed by tho Committee that Mr. Samuel Evans, M.P., one of the members, moved that copies be bought ond supplied to each member. The book has also timely interest in view of the .labour movement and the growth of Collectivist principles, for it contains a broad statement of a policy of social reform from one who is a well-known Free Trader. - THE PLEASURES OF' BALLOONING.

Princess Di Teano, in the current "Strand Magazine," has an interesting article, illustrated with bird's-eye view pictures of town and country, on the pleasures of ballooning. "My most exciting trip (she says) was one accom- panied by a certain amount of risk. We started from St. Cloud, Paris, in half a gale, M. Jacques Faure as aeronaut in charge, the other two passengers besides myself being Mrs.Assheton Harbord and Lord Royston. We chose six in the evening as the time of departure, our intention being to travel all night and land in Germany some time in the morning. Darkness came on very quickly, being greatly increased by the heavy rain-clouds that surrounded us on all sides. The wind became stronger and stronger, veering round to a regular south-westerly gale. The prospect was scarcely pleasing, and the next hours were somewhat critical ones. We could not tell whether we were already out of France, but the com- pass indicated that we were being driven towards the , north. The night was intensely black, and our skilled aeronaut judged that we were travelling at the tremend- ous rate of a hundred kilometres—about sixty-three miles—an hour. Every now and then we dashed into I some thick cloud that enveloped us like a fog for a few moments. The only sounds we could hear were the wind roaring in the trees beneath us and the patter of the rain on the balloon. Personally we were in the greatest possible comfort. There was not the slightest apparc it motion, not a breeze fanned our faces, for, of course, we were tiavelling with the hurricane, and the big balloon overheard kept the rain from us nicely. Under these circumstances we dined with a very good appetite, the only drawback being that, as ballast was running short cud a descent in such a hurricane not to be desired, we were obliged to hurriedly , threw overboard the remainder of our dinner land our provisions for the morning meal. Every now and then we passed over a conglomeration of lights that denoted tho presence of some small town or village, but no answer came to our shouts of 'On sommes-nons?' and the gale whirled us on into the night. "Eventually the voyagers descended in the softest of ploughed fields, and we scrambled out in a veritable quagmire. The sea was a hundred yards off, and we had landed on the coast of Holland, near a small village not far from Dordrecht, having accomplished ;the journey from Paris in four hours and a half.'

"I think that rain is the greatest enemy to balloon- ing, and it is really hopeless to struggle against a heavy downpour. The rain increases the weight of the balloon t) an enormous extent, and is for ever forcing her downwards. You throw ballast overboard in the most hopeless manner, for a rise of a few hundred feet is immediately followed bya proportionate sinking, and you are lucky when, having got rid of your store of ballast in an incredible short space of time, you find a safe spot for a descent."

div.head: WILD COUNTRY LIFE.
div.p: WILD COUNTRY LIFE.

A pair of golden eagles have recently appeared on a well-stocked grouse moor, and I hear that, in defiance of the Act strictly protecting them, the keepers are most anxious to "secure "them if they do not leave the moor at an early date. On` this particular moor one day recently I perceived a pair of eagles soaring along the hillside, the nearest bird being only a few yards off. My sudden movement caused her to soar abruptly up, the rush of the air through her wings being clearly heard. div.head: MESSRS. TUCK'S POSTCARDS.
div.p: MESSRS. TUCK'S POSTCARDS.

Messrs. Raphael Tuck and Sons, Limited, have just issued a fresh lot of their famous oilette and other coloured picture postcards, and some very choice i examples may now be found n the shops. This famous firm's range of postcard publications now exceeds 40,000 varieties, embracing every style and class of subject worthy of reproductien. Messrs. Tuck's" Home Decorations "competition should prove what a splendid outlet exists for the practical use of really artistic postcards, and the exhibition of the competing entries in .Tuly next in the Royal Institute of Painters in Water Colours, upon which the foremost Academicians have consented to adjudicate, will be a revelation to the public as to the artistic possibilities of carefully selected postcards. The first series of Asti Heads which was issued last year having proved so immensely successful—the sale of this charming set of six post- cards having run into hundreds of thousands of sets, the demand on the part of the public still unabated—it was but natural that the firm should follow it up with a second series. They have also added a packet of "Bridge Problems "Postcards, which were the innocent cause of the interesting case against "Punch,' which was decided by the Lord Chief Justice a week or two ago.

div.head: CURE FOR ASTHMA.
div.p: A CURE FOR ASTHMA.
A Noted Physician will Prove this to all Sufferers in the United Kingdom.

llt is but natural that the majority of SUfferers from Asthma, after trying doctors and numberless remedies without avail, have Come the zonclusion that there is no cure for this most distressing disease. These same persons may still have doubt when they learn through the columns of the press that Dr. Rudolph Schiffmann, the recognized authority who has treated more cases of Asthma than any living doctor, has at last achieved success. He has perfected a remedy whish not only gives immediate relief in the worst cases, but has posi- tively cured thousands of sufferers who were considered incurable. These persons had previously been just as sceptical as some of our readers now are. Dr.Schiff mann's remedy doubtless possesses the merit which is claimed for it, or he would not extend an invitation to every sufferer to make a free personal test of it. He authorizes this paper to announce that he is not only willing to give free to any person suffering from Asthma or Bronchitis in the United Kingdom, one free liberal "trial package" of his Cure, but urgently requests all sufferers to send him their name, to whom a sample will be posted absolutely free of charge. He fears that in making the claim he does for his Cure, a strong doubt may arise in the minds of many, and knows that a personal test, as he offers to all, will be more convincing, and prove its merits, than thousands of Testimonials which he could publish from persons who have been permanently cured by the use Of his remedy. "Dr. Schiffmann's Asthma Cure,"as it is called, has been sold by most chemists for several years, although many persons may never have heard of it, and it is with a view to reaching these that be makes this offer. This is certainly a most generous and fair offer, and all who are suffering from any of the above complaints should send to Dr. R. Schiffmann, British bepot, 3, Snow Hill, London, E.C. div.head: COMMERCIAL TRAVELLERS' DINNER.
div.p: COMMERCIAL TRAVELLERS' DINNER.
ALDERMAN PIERPO/NT AND
OPERATIOIS ON THE CONTINENT.

Warrington Commercial Travellers held their first annual dinner at the Lion Hot)]. on Saturday evening. The proceedings were under the auspices of the local Branch of the United Kingdom Commercial Travellers' Association and the enthusiasm which was displayed was eloquent testimony to the flourishing condition of this new organization. About sixty-five sat down to an excellent repast served by Mr. John Lee. Alderman Pierpoint (president) was at the head of the table and was supported by the Mayor and Mr. F. Coysh, general secretary of the Association. Letters of apology for non-attendance had been received from Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., and Mr. R. G. Bouldon, Southport.

div.head: TEIE TOAST LIST.
div.p: TEIE TOAST LIST.

The customary loyal toasts were honoured on the proposition of the CHAIRMAN. Mr. W. L. WALKER, proposed "The town and trade of Warrington,"coupling with it the name of the Mayor. From all that he could hear he thought that Warrington was sharing in the•wonderful wave of prosperity which was passing over the country. In Warrington they heard very little of the Unemployed Question, in fact at all times Warrington seemed to stand out by itself in that respect—(hear, hear)—as even during periods of depression trade was always good in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) The toast was heartily drunk. The MAYOR, in replying, said that commercial travellers had a great responsibility, as all the wealth which manufacturers could command was of little use unless they had capable men to sell their goods. His Worship proceeded to refer to the improvements which had been effected in Warrington during the last3o years. It was hoped that in t\velve months the Bridge-street widening scheme would be completed, and he hoped that in the near future Warrington Bridge would be replaced by a structure sixty feet wide. (Hear, bear.) He trusted that their association would prosper. (Applause.) ALDERMAN PIERPOINT AND CONTINENTAL

div.head: OPERATIONS.
div.p: OPERATIONS.

Alderman PIERPOIST submitted the toast of the Association. He had, he said, been a commercial traveller before many in that room were born. He did not think many covered as much ground as he did on behalf of his firm. Ile had to cover the whole of the European Continent and he would like to say that there were immense possibilities for cemmereial travellers on the Continent provided they studied the character of the country they were going to. They must be con- versant with the language and must enter into the minds of the people with whom they were doing business. If they desired to do business with a German firm they must follow out the German idea of business and not make the fatal mistake so many English travellers made of trying to force English ideas and monies down the throats of the foreigners. (Hear hear.) To his mind there was no reason why they should leave matters to the foreign traveller. If a foreign traveller came to England he could speak the English tongue and nnderstood our business methods, and he would advise them all to similarly study foreign countries. (Applause). Speak' of the Association, he said it seemed to him that there must he a necessity for such an organization. The tendency of commercial undertakings at the present time was in the direction of combination for the pur- pose of economy not only in production but in selling. Although he was not at the back of the heads of those people who proposed the formation of a soap combine, he thought the economy of selling would be in the employment of one traveller where before there were live, and for that reason, whilst he ISelieved that the combination was a fair one, he was glad that it had fallen through. He believed that the Travellers Com- bination was for the purpose of defence, and that there was in it no breath of defiance, and he agreed that labour had a perfect right to combine to defend itself. (Hear, hear.) He was delighted that a Branch of the Associa- tion had been formed in Warrington, and he would do all that he could to help forward the object which they had in view. (Applause). Replying to the toast, Councillor.W. F. BROONS, of Manchester, ennumerated the objects of the Associa- tion. These were, he said, to improve the lot of the commercial fraternity, look after the interests of the members when on the road, to give legal assistance, to help in times of trouble and necessity, to make special provision for insurance, endowments and sick pay and to cultivate good fellowship amongst its members. In regard to what had been done in the matter of insurance, the Association secured for him a special premium reduction which was three times as large as his annual subscription. It had also secured a reduction of cloak- room charges and further had enabled commercial travellers to obtain week-end return tickets at single fare. (Hear, hear). On the proposition of Mr. W. RARRArr the toast of the Warrington Branch of U.K.C.T.A., was heartily drunk.

Mr. .1. E. WARREN responded. The great success of the Branch, he said, would not have been achieved had it not been for the splendid manner in which they were served by their officers and especially by the secretary (Mr. Hayes). They had not to lose sight of the fact that a commercial traveller's life was short and that the present tendency on the part of big firms was to get young men about them, and he would advise them all to look forward to the time when they would be older and to see that by the time they were, if possible, independent or their own masters. They owed a duty to their employers but they must not forget their duty to themselves. As Shakespeare had said : To thine own self be true ; And it must follow as the night the day, . -
Thou canst not then be false to any man.—(Applause). Mr. H. MERCER submitted the toast of "The Commercial Travellers' Schools and Benevolent Institu- tion."

In responding Mr. F. COYSH said there was one quality which distinguished commercial travellers and that was charity, and this had ever been so as the first authentic traN'bller was the good Samaritan. The expenditure in both of their institutions was almost identical and stood at £13,000 per annum. When people heard that. they naturally concluded that both were working on a fairly large scale, but they could never translate the good which each did into terms of £. s. d. How could they in that way value the relief and benefit which the schools were to the widow and the fatherless children? How could they in terms of cost value the good which the children were to the community after they had passed through the schools? It was the proud boast of the management that the first failure amongst the children dealt with in the schools had yet to be recorded. (Applause.) The same thing applied to the Benevolent Institution and he recommended both to their hearty sympathy. Their support was one of the fundamental principles of the Association and he regretted that that plank of their platform did not receive the attention which it deserved. (Applause.) The toast of the " tisitors " was proposed -by Mr. A. G. BROWN and responded to by Mr. W. F. WHALLEY, and the health of the artistes was also cordially drunk.
During the evening songs were given by Messrs. J. Hill, A. E. Garner and H. W. Turner,, and humorous items by Mr. IL Hallard. Mr. B. Smith was the accompanist. •

div.head: TUIPERANCE REFORM.
div.p: TUIPERANCE REFORM.
MEETING AT BOLD-STREET WESLEYAN CHURCH. -- -- Disinterested Management Criticised.

The annual temperance meeting in connection with the Warrington Wesleyan Methodist circuit was held in Bold-street Church on Tuesday, Mr. C. E. Parker presiding over a fair attendanee. The principal speaker was the Rev. J. Alfred Sharp, connexional temperance secretary, and amongst others present were the Revs. Sidney Pitt, J. Manning and E.J. Gawne. The CHAIRNIAN said he was glad to think that the temperance cause was more alive to-day than it had been for a long time. They were told in the King's speech that a measure was to be introduced in the present Session dealing with the evils resulting from the sale of intoxicating liquors and it was a very important thing that all who valued the sobriety, righteousness, and well-being of the country should do ' what they could at this time to develop and strengthen temperance sentiment. If the Bill which was to be intro- duced by the Government was one likely to fulfil the purposes of all who wished to see a sober England, it I would be for them to give it a most strenuous backing. ' (Hear, hear). If, on the other hand, it was faulty and did not go as far as the country was prepared to go, it would be for them to express their disappointment and I see if it were not possible to strengthen the measure as I it went through the House. He thought that at the present time there was a greater recognition than he had I ever before known of the evils arising from intemperance I and the question was passing out of the region of mere I teetotalism and was becoming more and more a citizen's question. All classes of the community, whatever their personal habits might be in regard to intoxicating liquors, were realizing what a terrible drag on the wel- fare and prosperity of the country the abuse of intoxi- cating liquors was. There was a wider recognition than there had ever been before of the fact that each man was his brother's keeper and was responsible to God for his welfare. The Temperance I Legislation League in which' he (Mr. Parker) was much interested was designed to try and shape legislation and I it was rather a pity that the one question upon which many of them differed,disinterested management,should be so much to the fore in their talks on the League's , proposals. To his mind the question was not of very vital importance. He did not see that it would be very operative, because of the difficulty of the monopoly I value. It did not seem very likely that anyone like I himself who thoroughly believed in disinterested management, would be prepared to supply capital to buy out the monopoly value, and on the other hand he did not think any sane man would desire that the com- munity should pay the monopoly value of a licence and hand it over to certain managers. As far as he could judge, the question was not a very vital one. What was vital was that through the operations of the League there had been found a method of expression of temperance sentiment ' which none of the existing organizations were enabled to bring in. The adherents of the League represented a great body of opinion which they had not so far been able to get with them in temperance effort, and what to him was more important than the question of disinter- ested management was to give the right hand of fellow- ship to those who were willing to go a certain distance with them, because without the moderate opinion they of what might be called the extreme temperance party would not be able to carry their point. Mr. Parker proceeded to quote front articles on the drink evil written by Mr. George R. Sims, who referred specially to drinking amongst women, and to the terrible cruelty to which children were exposed when taken to public- houses by their mothers. It was time the Churches were awakening to their responsibility on the t question. He believed that the difficulty was not so much in unwillingness to work but in lack of knowledge as to what they should do. The difficulty of dealing with public houses was a very awkward one. They had about 203 public houses in Warrington and be believed if they were reduced by half it would not make a great deal of difference because there would be plenty of facilities in those which remained. The whole environ- ment of the poor in our town was bad and tended towards drunkenness. It was very difficult to get the public houses away from the people, but was it not possible to get the people away from the public houses? In War- rington they were organizing a Garden City Suburbs Company, and already they were being well supported with funds. Of course, the movement was not a teetotal one. Sir Gilbert Greenall had promised £l,OOO and other gentlemen were subscribing in a like manner. The intention was to build houses and take the people away from their environment and place them in healthier and better conditions. He believed that would be an effort in the direction of temperance reform and he hoped all who wished to help would communicate with him. The Rev. J. ALFRED SHARP deli vered an exceedingly interesting and powerful address. He said they would never be able to displace the publichouse until they replaced it. He would like to emphasise the grave duty of Town Councils in respect to this and kindred matters. He hoped to see the time, when the civic ; publichouse, without the drink but meeting the social instinct, would be found like the free library in every town. (Applause.) If all the existing laws were properly enforced by the Councils of the cities and towns in respect to housing' it would help towards a great temperance revival. The cause of temperance was but a part of that still greater question of social uplifting, reform, and reconstruction. He stood there as an ardent opponent of disinterested management and he would suggest that if it be impossible to carry the scheme out, as he gathered from the Chairman that it would even if the option were granted, it was the duty of the League to drop this debatable point at the present moment when they were face to face with the promised Government measure. Was it not their duty to drop every point that would tend to divide them and debar them from having that union of heart and , feeling which they must have in the presence of the enemy ? He trusted Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman , absolutely. He believed the Government was going to give them a comprehensive measure of temperance reform but he had had too much to do with political life and fighting not to know that if the Government gave them a lead, it had a right to expect a backing, and that could not he given if there was something in the temperance ranks which tended to division. Dis- interested management had been introduced at Christiana, Norway, a town very similar to Hull. In Hull, one of the most drunken of our English towns, there were 13 per 1,000 convictions for drunkenness while in Christiana. under disinterested management, there were 57 arrests and convictions per 1,000. He had no desire to exchange the 13 for the 37. (Applause.) At the same time he did not believe in the denunciation of the League which some of his friends had indulged in. Mr. Sharp proceeded to speak on drink in its relation to child life. He said that in , place of industrial brutality which had been largely removed by beneficent legislation they had the drink brutality which made the cry of the children even more bitter. We thought more nowadays of wasting a little capital than of wastine our humanity. One fourth of the total deaths every year in England and Wales were those of infants under twelve months old and in , 1894 137,479 babies never reached their second year. The wastage of child life was very largely owing to the drink evil. In the London hospitals children were dying by hundreds from alcoholic poisoning, and Sir William Broadbent said that for every child' that died as the result of drink a dozen others were damaged. The speaker showed how by drunkenness education was hampered, and children were cruelly treated. Before they could defend child life there must be stern and rigorous dealing with the drink trade. He would make it illegal for a child.to enter a public-house, and he he believed they coitld carry a law forbidding any parent to take a child in arms into a public- house. There would have to be from the lovers of citzenship an appeal in the name of God and humanity to the women of England. That appeal to mean anything must be on Christian lines, for he confessed that, Socialist though he was, he knew of no power in Socialism that could alter the life and change the heart of man and therefore he was a Christian. He wanted to see the power of Christianity brought to bear on these complex and perplexing problems for that was the only power which could solve them. (Applause.) The Rev. J. MANNING in thanking the chairman and speaker on behalf of the meeting, said Wesleyans represented a force in the community which ought to count for more than it did in temperance work. (Applause.)

div.head: Living on Ladders.
div.p: Living on Ladders.

A singular story was told at the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, when Jesse Astall, painter, 21, Vere-street, was charged with stealing, by means of a trick, from Margaret Booth, Laira-street,*a step-ladder of the value of 2s. Gd. He was further charged with stealing from Alice Ann Bothwell, Church-street, a step-ladder, valued at 25., and also a step-ladder from Councillor Duncan, Padgate-lane, valued at 4s. Superintendent Monaghan said that on January 21st, prisoner went to Mrs. Booth's house, and asked for the loan of her step-ladder for a few minutes, as he was doing a little " job " close by. He did not return with it, and sold it to a man named William Broad- hurst for is. On February 4th, he went to Um. Both- well and borrowed her ladder, which he also sold for ls. The day afterwards he went to Mr. Duncan's, and borrowed his ladder,'which he, as usual, sold for is. The thefis,were reportrd to the police, and P.C. Clough arrested prisoner, and brought him to the police station, where he pleaded guilty. There were several other cases against prisoner for stealing step- ladders in various parts of the town, in fact, prisoner had been living on step-ladders for a long time. He served a term of imprisonment last year for theft, and had had six months for neglecting his children:— Prisoner was sent to gaol for three months with hard abour.

div.head: FOR EXTINCTION.
div.p: FOR EXTINCTION.

The Licensing Committee of Ramsgate has decided to withhold eight licences owing to complaints that betting men frequent the premises, and a further seven with a view to their cases being referred to the East Rent Kensington Licensing Committee for extinction. The Committee farther decided to close all automatic machines which encouraged gambling, and to abolish automatic musical machines.

most highly prized of all decorations—the Victoria Cross. In asking him to unveil the memorial the committee could not have made a more appro- priate choice. It was under Sir Redvers Buller that the South Lancashire Regiment, which has long been closely identified with this town, fought in South Africa. They took part in the arduous operations which preceded the relief of Ladysmith and their gallant commander, Colonel O'Leary, fell at Pieter's Hill. The memorial will per- manently commemorate the devotion and self- sacrifice of the late Colonel and other South 'Lancashire soldiers who laid down their lives in that terrible campaign. Sir Redver's Bullet's visit will indeed be a notable event in the history of the town and every effort is being made to render the celebrations worthy of the great occasion.

Lady Frances Balfour has THE RAID ON THE said that, while personally Commorrs. she does not recommend assaults upon the House of Commons, she yet is glad to see the fillip which the crusade of the suffragettes has given to a not-too-progressive cauee. In six months they have perhaps done more for women's suffrage than the Society of Women's Suffrage, of which she is 'President, has done in forty years. Theadvertise-1 rnents of the last week will certainly serve to keep the movement well before the publie mind., Women from all parts of England went to London • for the Hyde Park demonstration on Saturday last, and Miss Annie Kenney, at the meeting which preceded the two raids on the House on the night following the opening of the second session, declared she would bring 1,000 -cotton operatives to town, and they would make their way by hook or by crook, to the floor of the House of Commons. Tuvo or three attempts on Wednesday from successive meetings were made to reach "the floor of the House of Commons," and fifty-nine of "the deputation " were arrested, not without confusions sustained .bv collision with the strong arm of the law. The 'King's Speech promises increased facilities for women to serve on local bodies. There are women of education and affairs whose experience would be invaluable on local authorities. The aspira- tion of Mrs. Desnard, " We want a better, cleaner world " is excellent but the methods of herself and her followers do not commend themselves so easily. We hold that their cause cannot be established by the violence of a relatively small number, but by the fact being made clear that the mass of women are sincerely desirous of the vote. This essential fact is by no means proved, 'Whereas it is incontestable that many women of -serious thought and sober mind who could and would use the franchise intelligently are dismayed by the violence of the self-appointed leaders of the suffrage movement. But whatever the results the latter do not intend that the Government should forget them.

Lord Charles Beresford has BeREP3ORD'S WAY. provided us with One more sensation. He has resigned and protested before—once when he was a Sea 'Lord in 1888, when he felt that the Navy was being kept at a strength inadequate to the require- ments of the Empire. He proved himself jnstitied in his action then; it remains to be seen how far he may do so now. It is as well to have a clear view of the situation. Sir A. K. Wilson will relinquish command of the Channel Fleet next month. The successor who, by his record, his proved ability, his position in the service, and the splendid . efficiency -of every unit of the -service he has ever commanded, is marked nut for the post before the eyes of all men is 'Lord Charles Beresford. It is not merely that he is a breezy, popular figure. There is the testi• mony of those who are competent to judge of the value of his life's work. He has everything to gain by accepting the command offered him by the Admiralty, for its definite refusal will mean that, in all probability, the sea will know him no more as the director of the mighty engines of war which plough its surface. That would be a loss to the national service that it is not pleasant to contemplate. Lord Charles has stood so long for all that is best in the Navy that it behoves us to examine closely the grounds which he considers justify him in declin- ing the command of the Channel Fleet except under conditions which, no to the present, the Board of Admiralty derline to concede. Lord Charles Beresford has calculated the strength of the Fleet which he considers necessary to defend home waters and he has come to the conclusion that the Channel Fleet, at the strength to which it will be reduced next month, will be inenfficient for the purpose. He should be a good judge— none perhaps better—and the fact that he has felt justified in refusing a position which would place the crown upon his life's work, and which would give him the greatest of all his opportunities for leaving a Permanent mark upon the British Navy, in which his career has been so distinguished, argues the strength of his convictions. On the other side of the sheet it should not be forgotten that the 'te(inction of the Channel Fleet—which will be the strongest maritime force afloat—is to be accom- panied by the organisation of a Home Fleet which will prove a valuable additiob to the provision for Zteme defence, and enable the Channel Fleet to Pursue the broader strategic policy for which it is designed. That is an important consideration,and it is now to be seen whether the Board of Admiralty will prefer their own plan or Lord Charles Beresford's services.
The Examiner Saturday, February 16, 1907.
