Mr. BiRnELL's eloquent OPPOSITION plea on Thursday night for TACTICS. a large policy of trust in the Irish people, will be re•echoed by every true patriot. The new CHIEF. SECRETARY FOR IRELAND, although he has been but a short time in office, and admits his lack of a thorough knowledge of Irish affairs, declares that he approaches his task "with a sympathetic heart.' Is not that just what Ireland wants ? The great mistake of English government has been that we have tried to Govern Ireland according to English ideas, that we have never understood the Irish character, and that acts and administration which seemed right to us have not been in quite the same light by the Irish people. It is futile for Mr. WALTER LONG to say that the announce- ment in the KING'S speech is a contradiction of previous statements at the General Election. Does he not remember Sir HENRY. CAMPBELL*. BANNERMAN'S famous Stirling Speech, in which he declared himself a believer in self-government for Ireland, and advised the Irish members to take what they could get, provided it was consistent with and led up to to the "larger policy ? " That declaration was long before the General Election, and was brought into more prominence by Lord ROSEBERY'S subsequent announcement at Bodmin that he could not fight under that banner; so it is now surely rather too late in the day to complain that a measure for an extension of some form of self-government to Ireland is a contradiction to General Election pledges. It is, of course, easy to understand Mr. WALTER LONGS'S anger. He became Chief Secretary for Ireland when it was found that Mr. GEORGE WYNDHAM and the then Viceroy of Ireland had become tainted with the policy of "governing Ireland according to Irish ideas." There were many Conservatives and Unionists more or less convinced that a policy of devolution was the best solution of the Irish difficulty; but when the Ulster members found out what was going on, they did not rest until they;had forced the resignation of Mr. GEORGE WYNDHAM. The " ascendancy party" was furious that there should be any suggestion of allowing the majority of Irishmen a voice in the government of their own country. It must not be forgotten, too, that Mr. LONG iS now himself an Irish member, and leader of the Orange party, and that he is expected to fulminate against any proposals which would let the majority rather than the minority have the dominating voice in the Government of Ireland. And yet Mr. LONG almost admits that the Government pro- posals will be practical proposals, but pleads that they cannot be so considered because they are only part of a policy to which the Opposition is opposed! Surely that is an admission that the PRIME MINISTER is exactly keeping the pledge he made at sterling? The Government proposals are practical pioposals, but they are to be opposed not because they mean separation, but because, they are not consistent with and lead up to the "larger policy ?" No one can truthfully plead that this part of the Government programme was not before the electors.

But it is evident from the speech of the ex CHIEF SECRETARY that the Opposition are going to adopt pretty much the same attitude towards Mr. BIRRELL'S Irish Bill that they adopted towards his Education Bill. That, they pleaded, was not before the country at the election, and called the House of Lord's to assist them to reject it, for they knew better what the country wanted when they returned such a huge Liberal majority than did the Liberal members of Parliament themselves. It would seem thit the process is to be repeated as through. The Opposition will claim to be the real representatives of the opinion of the country, and will, by the help of the House of Lords, prevent the Ministry from getting the rneastms they are pledged to pass put on the Statute Book. All of which is only another proof of the wisdom of the PRIME MINISTER in allocating the place of honour in the Session's Parliamentary programme to the question of curtailing the power of the House of Lords, and making the people's will paramount.

On Thursday next Warring- GENERAL BULLER'S ton will be honoured with VISIT, a visit from One of the nation's most popular heroes in the person of General Sir Redvers Buller, V.C., who comes to unveil the handsome memorial to fallen soldiers which has been erected in Queen's Gardens. We have no doubt that the distin- guished soldier will be receive i with that warm- hearted enthusiasm with which Lancashire people are wont to greet those who have done noble service for their country. div.head: Musical Evening at Crosfields'.
div.p: Musical Evening at Crosfields'.

On Monday evening the Crosfield Choirs and Orchestra gave their annual concert in the Works Dining Hall before a crowded audience of friends and fellow employees. The orchestra opened with Prout's Triumphal "march, the choir following with the inelodious part-song by German "The Chase." The next piece, the Valse " Frisson d' Amour " (C. de Rhynal) with its rapid and whimsical changes of tempo was a conductor's piece and gave Mr. F. H. Crossley the opportunity for a personal triumph. Miss E. Barnes was very good in "0 ! Peaceful England " from German's opera " Iferrie England." The following glee, Bishop's Now Tramp o'er Moss and Fell " suffered from the abstention of the soloist Miss C. Hastings. Next was a tuneful seleotion from "The Country Girl"- (Monckton). In this no doubt the orchestra was heard at its best. The choir had a delicate task in its next contribution Pinsuti's " The sea bath its Pearls " but one of which it acquitted itself fairly well: In the next item the song and chorus "The Yeomen of England" (also from " Merrie England ") Mr. E. Pownall gave a most agreeable performance, the not least meritorious feature of which was the enunciation—every syllable was clear and articulate. The quartet "Strange Adventure "from " Yeoman of the Gnat d " by Misses Hewitt and Woodland, and Messrs. Tynan and Cook received an encore which was perhaps well deserved —though it must be said that the soprano was a trifle sharp. The penultimate piece Faning's part gong "The Miller's Wooing" was probably the best com- bined performance of the choir and orchestra, while in the closing effort of the orchestra, Sousa's well- known march" Stars and Stripes" again proved its popularity by winning an encore. The whole perform- ance, which reflected the greatest credit on the partici- pants and especially on the conductor Mr. F. IT. Crossley, was enthusiastically ,received and proved most enjoyable in every way. 'Miss C. Newall was accompanist.

During a service at Rayleigh (Essex) Baptist Chap the Rev. Mr. Dyer asked all who felt they must cough to do so ad get it over, as he wished to get on with the service.
o - So large was the attendance at St. Peter's congrega- tional tea party on Mondoy that supplies ran short .and the commissariat department had an anxious time until more comestibles were obtained.

o The Town Clerk of Eye on Wednesday reported that the last loan of borrowed capital had been paid off, thus placing the Corporation in a position which no other Corporation in England could boast of, being free from debt. This is something for the Warrington Corporation to think of. My eye !

Temperance reformers are expecting much from the Government in view of thb announcement in the King's Speech that a licensing measure is to be intro- duced this Session. Now is the time to present a united front and be ready .to support thg Ministry in any real reform which is proposed. o a We hope everybody will make an effort to fall in with the Mayor's wish that the occasion of General Buller's visit shall be observed as a half-holiday. The banks schools, and most of the shops will close, and it is suggested that employers of labour should also endeavour to grant a holiday to their workpeople.

* * Councillor Fred Stott missed a pleasant surprise on Tuesday evening. The members of the Trades and Labour Council had arranged to present him with a clock and bronzes in recognition of his devoted services as secretary. However Councillor Stott waS engaged in municipal business and could not attend the meeting, so the interesting ceremony had to be postponed.

* * "No reader can imagine himself at home in a library where an ()Moja' always interposes between him and the shelves ; such formality is chilling to the soul and fatal to that free adventurousness of spirit which makes the lover of books. The true function of the librarian is not to keep the readers apart from the books but to bring the two together.' —" Man- chester Guardian."

* * * A proposal to placard the street hoardings with hills detailing the effects of the abuse of alcohol was strongly opposed by Labour and Irish members of the Liverpool City Council on Wednesday as a reflection on the habits of the working man. As a result of an amendment they carried (amid laughter), the bill is not only to be put on the hoardings, but copies of it are to be distributed to "the high-class clubs and hotels of the city "as well. And why not!

* ; * Mr. Dodds and Councillor Pemberton had a very cordial reception at a meeting of Manchester rate- payers on Monday evening, when they related briefly what had been done in Warrington ta stop illegal and improper trading. .r Some of the revelations which are common knowledge in Warrington quite startled the Manchester people, and there is no doubt they were impressed with the necessity for a watchful Rate- payers' Association to keep a check on expenditure and with the power of public opinion when properly roused against the abuses of municipal Government.

* * The ingenious simplicity of Jesse Astall's mode of existence compels admiration. At the Police Court on Tuesday he was sent to gaol for "living on ladders." His method was to call at houses and borrow the family step-ladders for a few minutes "for a job close by." The lader was generally lent willingly and promptly sold by Jesse fords. He found ladders so easy to get and so easy to sell that he has" lived' on them for some tine. Now he has gone to goal for three months, and if the treadmill were still in existence he might • extend his acquaintance with ladders in a different direction.

* * The Rev. J. Alfred Sharp, connexional temperance secretary to the Wesleyan IfethodW Community, is an interesting and racy speaker and his address at the temperance meeting at Bold-street Church on Tuesday evening was one of the best we have listened to for some time. Although many of his remarks were couched in lighter vein, he did not lose sight of the serious aspect of this great question and he made a very powerful appeal on behalf of the children who suffer through the drink evil. We hope his remarks will have the effect of stimulating temperance activity which has been particularly marked in the town of late.

o The latest .figures are to hand showing the amount of tobacco used—and abused—annually in Europe and America. In the former continent the yearly consump- tion is estimated at something over two and a quarter pounds to each inhabitant. Taking each country, the position is thus :—Holland smokes the comparatively enormous amount of 7 pounds average per person., Austria- Hungary 3.8 pounds, Denmark 3.7, Switzer- land 3.3, Belgium 3.2, Germany 3, Norway 2.3. France 2.1, Sweden nearly 2, British Isles 1.3 i, Italy 1.25, Spain 1.7 and Russia 1.2. For the Balkans there are no returns. In the United States the proportion is greater than that of any European country except Holland, being no less than 41 pounds to each inhabi- tant. * * *

One of the greatest difficulties which the temperance reformers have to face is the fact that they have no good substitute to offer in place of the social attrac- tions of the public-house. At Battersea the problem has been to a great extent solved by the Borough Council which provides a municipal recreation room. On Wednesday the purchase of a second billiard table for the room was sanctioned and one of the members in suppirting the proposal said "that in such a district where there were 91 licensed premises in a small area, it was right and proper that the working men should have reasonable recreation apart from the influence of the public-house. ,The billiard-room was the safest place in which a wonEn could leave her husband, and he hoped to see the recreation room twice its present I size.'

* We fear that Mr. R. Pierpoint's services in Parlia- ment have been under-estimated though we do not suggest that the verdict of Warrington just over 12 months ago was wrong. It was very rarely that anything was heard of the late member when he represented the borough at West- minster, but he did more than the daily press chronicled. When the Irish row occurred in 1893, Mr. Pierpoint—according to the reminiscences to which he treated the "Lit and Phil" on Monday practically saved the life of Colonel Saunderson, who was in the grip of a wild Irishman, by seizing the latter by the throat and holding him at arm's length. On another occasion Mr. Pierpoint attempted at 4.30 in the afternoon to catch the Speaker's eye, but did not succeed until ten minutes to ten when he had risen for the fourteenth time. This was equally heroic of him. We wonder if it was the claims of Cyprus which were pressing keenly upcu the late "Member. By the way it would not be a bad idea if Mr. Pierpoint took the island in the near east as the subject of his next lecture.

" Please, ma'am," the said, "do von want a nice rabbit to-day?" The mistress was severe. " Certainly not ; haven't I told you that I will not buy from street hawkers ? " The maid was not abashed. "But he's got it in his pocket," she said, with a fine suggestion of mystery. "In his pocket ? What has that to do with it?" The maid merely answered, "They're the best kind, ma'am ; it's a real chance." There was something to be cleared up here, and a more detailed cross-examination of the girl threw a queer light on back-door trading. 13riefiy, the girl's mysterious hints meant that the man at the door with a rabbit was a poacher or a poacher's agent, and here was a good chance to get a rabbit that was really fresh-killed--one that might have been nibbling grass in Cheshire within twenty-four hours. The new maid had come from a house where plached rabbits were regularly bought, and for the benefit of her new mistress she explained the signficance of the fact that the man liad the rabbit in his pocket. When a man comes to the door with a dozen rabbits dangling on his arm, it seems, he is an honest fellow selling imported rabbits, which he buys cheaply in the market. But if he comes with bulging pockets the probability is that he has not come by his rabbit in a strictly legal way of business. Poachers are so accustomed to stealth that even when they have carried their catch far beyond the reach of the game- keeper or the rural policeman they still shrink from publicity.—" Manchester Guardian."

Warrington and the Ship Canal. A representative meeting of the traders of Warring- ton and the Rivers Committee of the Council was held at the Town Hall yesterday afternoon to discuss the proposals contained in the Manchester Ship Canal Bill of 1907. After a long discussion it was decided that the proposals were prejudicial to the interests of the town and the Corporation was requested •to petition against the measure. We understand that the petition will be lodged on Monday. Popular Penny Concert. An excellent programme was given at the popular penny concert in the Bold-street Wesleyan School- room on Saturday evening. The Rev. j. Manning presided over a crowded attendance. The Leidertafel Glee Singers had been engaged, and their selections were greatly appreciated. Mr. Houghton Brazendale's Quartette Party from Manchester, also gate songs, duets, quartettes and humorous sketches in admirable style. A Warning to Householders. A daring instance of housebreaking which affords a salutory lesson to householders who do not properly secure their premises during a brief absence. has been reported to the Stockton Heath police. On Wednesday afternoon the house of Mr. Downes, " Glearoy," Fair- field-road was left unattended and not properly secured and during this period housebreakers effected an entrance and mide off with several pounds' worth of jewellery. Up3n the theft being discovered the police were informed, but up to the present they have been unable to trace the culprit. GENERAL BULLER'S VISIT.—For sate or hire, National Flags, Streamers, Shields, etc. Large stock.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge-st.—Advt. Newsagents' Dinner. The first annual dinner in eonnectiou with the War- rington Branch of the Retail Newsagents' Book- sellers' and Stationers' Union, was held on Thursday evening at Bibby's Cafe, Market-street, when about 25 sat down to an excellent repast. A. smoking concert followed the proceedings, which were under the chairmanship of Mr. T. Locker. Enjoyable musical items were given by Messrs. Horrobin, D. Gittens, T. Forbes, T. Locker, W. Litherland, J. G orse, Halliwell, and Mr. J. W. Critchley, whilst Mr. Smith contributed humorous recitations. Mesers. Critchley and Gorse acted as accompanists. School Attendance Summones. The Cheshire County Education Committee, at a meeting at Crewe, on Monday, discussed the question whether school attendance officers or police should serve summonses on parents who neglected to send their children to school. The Standing Joint Com- mittee of the county sent to the education authority a resolution stating that it was not desirable that school attendance summones should be served by the police, and recommending that all such summonses should be served by school attendance officers. After a long discussion, the committee decided by 14 to 9 that the police should service school attendance summonses. Farm Fire—Supposed Incendiarism. A: destructive fire occurred on Wednesday night at the farm of Mr. Ff. Brocklehnrst, Road Side Farm, .Stretton, near Warrington Shortly after five o'clock flames were seen issuing from a large Dutch barn containing wheat, oats, &c. The Warrington and Wilderspool brigades were summoned, and on arrival found that the fire had secured a firm hold of the barn. The flames, fanned by a northerly wind, spread with alarming rapidity, and a large stack of hay adjoining was soon blazing furiously. The task of the firemen was one of considerable difficulty, but a good supply of water being obtainable, they directed their efforts in saving adjoining farm buildings, and it was only after, several hours hard work that they were successful. The produce in the barn and the stack were totally destroyed as well as alnumber of valuable farming implements. The damage is estimated at nearly £l,OOO and is fully covered by insurance. The cause of the outbreak is at present unknown, but it is sup- posed to be the work of an incendiary. Capital and Labour. There was an excellent attendance at the weekly meeting of the Warrington Junior Liberal Association , which was held 41 Gregory's Cafe, Buttermarket- street on Monday evening, when a debate on "Are capital and labour essentially antagonistic ? " took , place with the Progressive Lab our League. Coun- cillor Hawthorn presided. Mr. J. Morton led off for the Progressive Labour League, and said they were I not essentially( antagonistic. If they thought for a short time of the complex nature of society, and the many and varied opinions about reforms an individual might hold, they would see at once how very complicated the industrial system must be with- out a proper organization. Some people held that competition in industry was an excellent thing, while there were others who believed that our social condi- tions would never have arrived at a proper state until competition was completely banished. The labourer had to sell his labour for the highest price he could obtain and there was nothing to guide him bat the market rates. apitalists were bound to buy .at the lowest price at which they could get labour, and consumers purchased produce for as little as they could. It was their duty to endeavour to get such legislation as would ameliorate the unhappy conditions which existed. (Applause.)—.Mr. H. Gray ceatended that capital and labour were antagonistic. They could never blot out Icompetition, but Mr. Morton had used competition in a very narrow sense indeed. He thought that by class 'legislation for some time to come they would approximate to the general happiness of the com- munity. • (Applause;) A discussion afterwards took place in which Messrs. Kendrick, Richard Osborne, Adams, Derbyshire, Pook, Morton and Rowlands took place.

GARLAND, Ironmongerßride st., Warrington.—Advt. "Wireless Telegraphy." Before the Warrington Science Students' Associa- tion on Saturday an interesting lecture was delivered on" Wireless telegraphy" by Mr. R.H. Albery, in the Technical Institute. The Chairman was Mr. P. Fisher. The lecturer commenced his subject by tracing its origin from the time Of Herodotus, when torches were used for signalling, to the twentieth century, when we are all familiar with the Wireless form of telegraphy perfected by Signor Marconi. By means of experiments and lantern slides he explainei how it was that a messnge could be received by a peason, when the origin was some distance away. He showed how electric waves travelled in parallel straight lines, and how they only differed from light arel sound waves in the number of vibrations per second, those of electricity being two millions per second. In con- cluding he caused a bell to ring in one room when the battery was in an adjoining room. After the lecture, a vote of thanks was proposed by Mr. Wicks, seconded by Mr. Newton, and carried unanimously. LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SHOES, UNDER THE CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—Adtv. Dancing was commenced at 8, and continued until 2 a.m., over 100 couples being present, including the Mayor (Alderman Smethurst), Councillors Lord, Cannington, and Dickinson (mem- bers of the Markets Committee). Handball. Warrington Gymnasium Haqdball Team journeyed to Port Sunlight a week last night (Friday) to fulfil their engagement with the Soap Team. In the open- ing stages of the game, Sunlight had more of the play than the Wirepullers, but failed td put the necessary finishing touches to their riaovemerite. After a while Warrington fairly took the Play, and were not long in registering the Ist goal by Holloway, from a penalty throw. From some very quick passing movements amongst the forwards, Bibby secured two further goals, and later, Warrington being awarded another penalty, Holloway, with his usual accuracy, secured the fourth pal. In the 2nd half, Warrington, again resumed the attack, the backs tackling keenly, and the forwards passing well. •Woods, as loose forward, both tackled well, and made some grand openings. Further goals for the visiting team were secured by Regan 2, Bibby 1, and Woods 1. Warring- ton came away winners with the pleasing result, 8 goals to 2. The next league match will take place at Myrtle-street Gymnasium, Liverpool, on Wednesday night next, February 20th, when Warrington, fulfil heir return engag3n3nt with Liverpnl. PIII3LIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCA.SHrRE.—Advt. Land Nationalization. Delegates for the Warrington Women's Liberal Association, who attended Lancashire Conference on Public Landownership held at Manchester last month, presented thier reports at a meeting of the Association on Monday. The four ladies deputed to attend the meeting were Mrs. Sampson, Mrs. Osborne. Mrs. Felix Maginn, and Mrs. John Maginn. —" Land Nationaliza- tion" said the delegates who reported—Mrs Osborne and Mrs Sampson— appears to be the only solution of the land problem and it would be advisable for the association to arrange for a lecture so that the whole question could be discussed. The land ought to be, as was first intended, the common property of the people instead of which four-fifths was owned by 500 men in the House of Lords. It was quite evident therefore that the people would have to concentrate their efforts in a united challenge to that austere assembly and that justice and-equity should be the main issues If land were the common property of the state there would be less congestioi and slums would be abolished; the people would be able to live in healthy homes had the children would have a fair chance of growing up into healthy men and women. It was very necessary for them as an Association to ally themselves with the movement and accord it their hearty support, The delegates were heartily thanked for their services. Latchford Wesley Guild. A lecture illustrated by lantern slides was given in the Wesleyan Caurch on Thursday evening by the Rev. Joseph Manning entitled "Mimicry in nature," Councillor Luke Ellison, J.P., occupied the chair, and in his introductory remarks emphasised the value of the Wesley Guild as an auxiliary of the Methodist Church. The lecture was then proceeded with and Mr. Manning glve some striking examples of the wonderful adaptation of various insects and animals to their environment, which were lucidly demonstrated by the aid of the clear lantern slides thrown on the screen. A cordial vote of thanks to lecturer and chairmln concluded an interesting evening.

Tenant farmers on the large Cheshire estate of Lord Egerton of Tatton have received the following letter from his lordship :—" I have to-day instructed my agent to hand you formal notice to quit, which has been rendered necessary by a desire to cancel the present agreement, and to substitute for it a simpler form which will be in harmony with recent legislation. I trust that the cordial relations which have long existed batweert us will not in any way be affected by the new Agricultural Holdings Act, 1903,which comes into operation on January Ist, 100)." ISo startled was L•ninax by the appearance of the defendant, that he did not-speak to him, and Harrop immediately disappearei from view. For the defence it was cmtended that defendant was not in the works lat all, but at the time stated he was at home quarell- ; ing with his wife.

THE MEETINGS FOR MEN. " Future Punishment' "Future punishment : Is it everlasting ?" was the subject of the weekly address on Thursday evening by the Rev. J. F. Matthews at Toft's Assembly Room. The room was, as usual, full, and keen interest was taken in the subject.—Mr. Matthews began by pointing out the complexity of the whole subject of eschatology. At least three theories had their avowed adherents, each class claiming New Testament authority for the posi- tionsheld. Some taught the" Everlasting Punishment" of the wicked; some the " Larger Elope," while a few favoured "Conditional Immortality.' Besides asking "What did the Bible sly " they had another question to answer," Did it mean exactly what it said ? ' It was an oriental book, with an oriental colouring. Men spoke and thought in metaphor, simile, parable and picture, so that a strict and careful exegesis had to be combined with a large insight into the meaning of many Scriptures if full justice was to be done to truth. These qualities were greatly needed in dealing with such a subject as future punishment. Mr. Matthews said they were all familiar with the idea of punish- ment.

WIDNES CURATE'S APPOINMENE The Rev. S. Hilton. curate of Farnworth Parish Church, has been appointed aortae of t. Andrew's, Sonthport, in succession to the Rev.F. G. Goddard, and will take up his duties shortly after Easter. WIDNES AGENT'S DEATH.

I Mr. John Valentine, who had been a well-known figure, in St. Helens, Widnes, and Garston. for nearly forty years, died on Wednesday. at his residence, Wood- ' croft, Halton View, Widnes. Mr. Valentine had for over thirty-nine years acted as agent and traveller for • Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Company. St. Helens. IHe was sixty-seven years of age, but had been in feeble health for some time. Some years ago Mr. Valentine ' was the recipient of a most valuable present from the licensed victuallers of Widnes and district. He leaves a widow,three sons, and three daughters to mourn his loss.

div.head: WIDNES BOXERS WIN.
div.p: WIDNES BOXERS WIN.

, At the Liverpool Gymnastic Club on Thursday last week two boxing matches in which Widoesians were keenly interested, took place. The first was between Hugh Doyle, of Widnes, and Paddy Carroll, of ' Liverpool. Carroll was the favourite at the opening, but Doyle forced the pace at the middle and finish of the contest and won a well merited victory on points. , The feature of the programme was a twenty-round contest for £5O a side and a purse of £6O between T. t Burns, of Widnes, and W. Morgan, of London. The men were physically well matched, and Morgan being slightly the heavier. Burns had much the better of the contest, and was awarded a popular verdict on points.

div.head: NEW BRIDGE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE NEW BRIDGE AT RUNCORN.

The members of the Liverpool Municipal Technical Students' Association were favoured on Saturday evening with a lecture on "The Evolution of Bridges" by Mr. J. Wilding, surveyor, of Runcorn. Mr. W. T. Emery presiding. The lecturer gave a resume of many of the methods employed in the construction of bridges of olden type. He showed by various examples how great ingenuity had been cultivated in mastering problems of bridge construction, and further pointed out how the simpler ideas had developed to be the chief factors of consideration in modern bridges. The lecture was copiously illustrated by many interesting lantern slides.

div.head: RUNCORN LICENSING SESSIONS.
div.p: RUNCORN LICENSING SESSIONS.

IThe annual licensing- sessions for the Runcorn police division were held on Monday.—Superintendent Ennion, in his report, said there were forty-four licensed . victuallers, fifty bsersellers, and three others who sell ; off the premises, givina an average of 217 of the popula- tion to each house. Daring the year four licensed ' houses had been closed, namely, the Volunteer Inn, Three Crowns Inn and Crimea Tavern, and a confec- tioner's licence. Inn, hundred and thirty-one persons had been proceeded against for drunkenness. and 111 convicted, as compared with 132 proceeded against, and 115 convicted in the preceding year. Sixty of these persons were non-residents. The whole of the licensed premises in the division had been well conducted, and the police did not object to the renewal of any of the existing licences.—The whole of the old licenses were renewed, tind there were no applications for new ones. The licence of the Anchor Inn, Halton-road, was trans- ferred to Mrs. George Horsefield, and the Holyhead Harbour to Mr. William Mercer. DROWNING FATALITY.

Mr. R. Dodson, district coroner, held an inquiry at the Runcorn Courthouse on Nfonday into the circum- stances attending the death of William Morgan, dock labourer, whose body was recovered from number four- lock of the old line of the Bridgewater Canal on Saturday afternoon.—Edward Webster, dock labourer, 12, Trentham-street, said the deceased lodged with him. He also was a dock labourer. He was about 62 years of age. On Friday morning at 6.20 they left the house together. Witness went to the docks and the deceased said he would have a glass of whisky and bade witness good morning. He had previously remarked that he did not feel very well. rhe pavements were a little slippery. The morning was dark. Deceased was short- sighted.—John Parr. locktenter, Crescent-cottage' said he saw deceased at 6.20 on Friday morning close to his hut and watched him cross th lock gates. He heard no splash. Deceased would have a second pair of lock gates to cross.—William Byfield, captain of the Run- corn Grapplinz and Life Saving Corps, said he com- menced to grapple shortly after eleven o'clock on Saturday morning, and recovered the body at three o'clock in the afternoon from number four lock of the Old line of the Bridgew,.ter Canal. He helped to con- vey the body to the mortuary.—P.C. Wareing said he examined the body. There were cut marks on the face and head. He attributed them to the passing boats. The deceased's cap was found near number three lock and the body must have been shifted into the next lock. —A verdict of" Found drowned " was returned.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
TEIE TATE SIR, DWID GANIBL-4 MEMORIAL REFERENCES.

References to the great loss to the community by the death of Sir David Gamble, Bart., K.C.8., were made at practically all the places of worship in St. Helens on Sunday. The Dead March was played at most of the churches, and special memorial services were held at the Parish Church and St. Mark's. The Rev. Cyril Bardsley, vicar of St. Helens, who preached to a large congregation at the Parish Church in the morning from the words," A good name is better than precious oint- ment," said that during the past week the whole town and district had been moved by a common sorrow. The death of a single man had been regarded as a public calamity. Death had felled no ordinary tree, one who had been deeply respected and much loved had been removed from their midst, and that morning there was one predominating thought throughout the church. They shrank from the thought of their mortality, but they had been reminded of it. He prayed that God would give the townspeople grace to learn the intended lesson, a good name was better than precious ointment. Much had been written of Sir .David Gamble. The newspapers had joined in a tribute to his conspicuous ' gifts and transparent virtues. He was a great man, and better still he was a good man. Sir David was a man of &reat shrewdness and of abilities far above those of moft men, but his success in life was because those gifts were the instruments of an indomitable ,will and the consistent hard work of a high idea of responsibility. As a business man, as a municipal leader, and as a Volunteer officer he was always painstaking, zealous and untiring. His life was an inspiration to those who followed him. One thing that his life taught every man was" Whatsoever thine hand doeth, do it with all thy might." St. Helens passed through its most important epoch under Sir David's guidance. He knew no class distinctions. He was courteous and sympathetic to all. He loved St. Helens. and nothing gave him greater pleasure than to know that the love was shared by the people whom he met. As they looked back upon a life and a personality which so impressed I the commonity they saw that to ability was added zeal, to power there was added wisdom, to wealth there was added simplicity, and to strength there was added love. His life was ended but not his work, for of such men it was said "Their works do follow them."—The Rev. T. ,W. Ketchlee, vicar of St. Mark's, preached from the text, "What think ye of Christ," and referred to Sir , David's life and the remarkable demonstration of sympathy thatt had been manifested by the whole town ! during the week. div.head: FATAL FALL IN A GLASSWORKS.
div.p: FATAL FALL IN A GLASSWORKS.

At St. Helens, on Monday, Mr. Brighouse, County' Coroner, inquired into the death of John Brown, aged forty-four, of 14, Salisbury-street, who died in the St. Helens Hospital on Thursday last,from injuries received at Messrs. Pilkington Bros.' plate-glass works.—Tlaa Coroner said Brown and another man were working at 'the extensions of the Cowley Hill Works. They were excavating for t. new furnace, and the two men were ois platform about twenty feet above the excavation, aeceiving barrows full of dirt, which were hoisted up by an electric hoist, when deceased overbalanced and fell off the stage,fracturing his snine and wrist and damaging his ribs.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accident,' but suggested that the platform ought to be made wider.

div.head: BAND OF, ROBBERS.
div.p: A BAND OF, ROBBERS.

Seven prisoners were charged at St. Helens on Satur- day with breaking into a draper's van and stealing articles worth £6. Joseph Skelly, of Russell-street, was discharged.—John Wood, of 23 Hardy-street,Joseph Ledwith, Dennis Scully, and Peter Dolan were charged on the main count, while Wood's brother Patrick and his mother were charged with receiving £3 worth of the goods.—The Chief Constable stated that on the previous Saturday night a widow named Sarah Jane Hand left her van, as usual, in the yard of the Star Hotel, Liverpool-road, and it was afterwards broken into. The police, after making a number of inquiries, raided nine homes simultaneously. The bulk of the stolen articles were found at the house of the prisoner Wood.—Ledwith's brother said he wanted to make a complaint against the Chief Constable. What right had he to stop food going in to unconvicted prisoners ? He had no business whatever to do that.—The Chief Con- stable said they had found all kinds of things secreted in the food and drink that were brought to the prisoners, and there was an order from the Home Office that not only the prisoners but everything that was brought in to them hsd to he strictly searched. The prisoners had been provided with plenty of food.— Ledwith was then escorted out of the court shouting. —The six prisoners were sentenced to two months each.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
WOMEN'S LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
A meeting was held in the Primitive Schoolroom on Monday, Miss Allatt presiding, when a paper was read by Mrs. E. Bebbington. on "The Education Question," showing how it most affected women.

YOUNG MEN'S CATEIOLEC ASSOCIATION—"*". A social was held in the Assembly Rooms on Monday evening, under the auspices of the above society, an efficient band being in attendance. The duties of M.C. were very ably performed by Mr. James Swift, who gave an exhibition dance and performances on the mandoline. Mr. Kenny, as hon. secretary, is to be con- gratutated on the manner in which the function was carried out.

div.head: CONCERT AT HAYDOCK.
div.p: CONCERT AT HAYDOCK.

A concert was held at the Colliery Schools, Haydock, on Saturday evening in aid of St. Mark's Church Build- ing Fund. Mr. Lionel E. Pilkington presided, and the following artistes deserve great praise :—Miss Kate Turner, soprano; Miss Ethel Wynne-Jones, contralto; Mr. Walter Robertson, tenor; Mr. Hamilton Harris, bass; Master Alfred Barker Russian, violinist; humorist, Mr. Schofield Roberts ; pianist, Mr. Charles Kelly.

div.head: CARTERS' UNION.
div.p: CARTERS' UNION.

The Amalgamated Carters, Lurrymen, and Motor- men's Union held their annual tea meeting on Saturday, at the Prince of Wales Hotel, where an excellent knife- and-fork tea was provided for a large number of mem- bers. An address was given by Councillor Parr, of Bolton, which was listened to with great interest, and a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer,after which a capital concert was given and thoroughly enjoyed.
EARLESTOWN FOOTBALL PLAYERS ENTERTAINED.

The presentation of medals to the Earlestown Foot- ball team, winners of the Lancashire Junior Cup, at their headquarters, the Railway Hotel, was preceded by a dinner given by the wife of the President, Mrs. T. Siddeley. The cup occupied the place of honour, and was surrounded by the medals, which were afterwards presented by Mr. G. Appleton, father of Mrs. Siddeley, and one of the oldest residents in Earlestown. Songs were afterwards given, and votes of thanks passed to Mr. and Mrs. Siddeley and Mr. Appleton.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE WORKING MEN'S ASSOCIATION.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE WORKING MEN'S ASSOCIATION.

A smoking concert was held on Saturday evening At the Conservative Club, Mr. G. F. Clarke presiding, when a programme of considerable merit was gone through, all the artistes being members of the club. The piano- forte solos by Mr. R. S. Norman were well received. §ongs, "Down the vale" and "The deathless army," were rendered by Mr. J. Nichols, and" Till death," by Nlr. J. Molyneux. Humorous songs were supplied by Mr. T. Curran. Mr. C. H. Lea sang "Star of the desert," and Messrs. J. Nichols and Lea the duet, " army and Navy." Mr. W. Sutton's recitations were. appreciated.

div.head: GILCHRIST LECTURES.
div.p: THE GILCHRIST LECTURES.

The third of the series of Gilchrist Lectures was given on Monday evening by Mr. R. D. Roberts in the Town Hall. Mr. Arthur Smith presided and introduced the lecturer. The subject," Gorges and Canons," was illustrated with limelight views, some in natural colours prepared from photographs taken by the lecturer during a visit to the regions described in 1901. He gave a full description of the Yellowstone Park, U.S.A. and of its volcanic character, the drainage of the district before the volcanic outbreak; the gorge of the Yellow- stone River,its striking features and gorgeous colouring, exploration and descent of the canon by Powell's expedition in 1859, the great proportions of its walla' brilliant colouring and ornamentation.

div.head: MR. J. A. SEDDON, M.P., AT EARLESTOWN4
div.p: MR. J. A. SEDDON, M.P., AT EARLESTOWN4

Mr. J. A. Seddon, Labour member for the Newton Division, who is conducting a series of visits to trades union lodges in the division, on Saturdny evening was the guest of the Earlestown Waggonmakers' Society. He said that the Labour party would put up a fight. with the Government if old age pensions was not men- tioned in the King's Speech, and declared that whatever might be the claims for rebate in taxation they were determined that old men and women should have first. consideration, for justice to them was long overdue The finances of the country warranted a saner poor law administration than the present brutal, brainless, heart- less system. He refused to prophesy what the Labour party would do with respect to the House of Lords, but the present constittion of it, in his opinion, was an anomaly and cowardly assembly. If it „would enable the Labour party to have a stand-up fight its days would be numbered.

DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. THOMAS WOOD. The death occurred on Saturday of Mr. Thomas Wood, licensee of the Hand and Banner Hotel, Newton- le-Willows following upon a lingering,' illness daring the past three or four years. Prior to coming to Newton Mr. Wood carriedon the business of a -tobacconist at Earlestown, and had managed the Ram's Head Hotel for Mr. Forster. In the township be was very well respected and though his death, at a comparatively early age, 37 years, was not. altogether unexpected, it has caused great regret and sorrow to his relatives and friends. Mr. Wood was Freemason of the Lodge of Faith 494, Ashton-in-Maker- field. He has left a widow and one child. The funeral took place on Wednesday afternoon at the Newton-in- -I%lakerfteld cemetery, Bro. the Rev. J. Rider,vicar of St. Peter's officiatihg. In addition to Mrs.,Wood,Mr:and Mrs. Baker (Winwick), and other relatives present, deceased's fellow Freemasons were represented by Bros. F. Harwood, P.P.0.P., J. Wright, P.M., T. Bowes, 1.P.M., T. Ritchie, P.M.. H. A. Hibbert, S.D., E. Jones, ID., J. T. Hoggard, LG., J. Waldron, S.S., %V. Singleton,J.S, %V. Welsh, T. Lythgoe, W. Sherrington J. Taylor, and A. Smethurst (484), J. Crouchlev (2(55 Newton), and Aukland (1250" Gilbert Greenall ;' Lodge, Warringxm) The local Licensed Victuallers' Association was repre- sented by Messrs. C. A. Owen, G. Sturgess, T. Board- man, T. Chapman, .T. Millar, E. Wainwright. There were also present—Messrs. W. Hayes, S. Davenport, H. Buckley, S. Rimrner, P. Percival, G. Naylor, represent- ing the tradesmen, and others. Bros. T. Bowes, T. 'Ritchie, J. T. Hoggard, and W. Singleton were the Masonic bearers. Wreaths were forwarded, in addition to the relatives, by the Freemasons and Licensed I Victuallers.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

Tme MEASLES EPIDEMIC.—Owing to the continuance of the epidemic of measles among the children the Medical OtHoer of Health, Dr. Sephton, has closed the National School for another fourteen days. Both the Church and Wesleyan Sunday schools will also remain closed next Sunday. CONCERT.—A large and appreciative audience assembled in the Padgate National School last Friday evening, when e concert% organixed by Miss Birtles, was given in aid of the District Nurse Fund. The ladies' orchestra, under the capable leadership of Mrs. W. B. Roberts, rendered several excellent selections of music, —theintermezzo and "The whistler and his dog," being perhaps the most takitig items, while the toy symphony was very amusing, Mr. Victor Roberts, who assumed the role of conductor, making the audience roar with. his antics. Miss Lillie Birtles, who has a very sweet. voice, sang "The wreath' very nicely, while Miss Daunt was very successful in her rendering of " Carmena." Miss Gertrude Henshall recited with ' much elocutionary power and expression. The humorous element was in the hands of Messrs. Victor Roberts anl H. M. Ashton, who were both very successful. Mrs. Roberts delighted the audience with a violin solo. Miss Birtles and all artistes were accorded a hearty- vote of thanks, on the motion of the Rev. William Mellor, resident Wesleyan minister, s(conded by Colonel Buckton.

FAIRY SHIP,
Kihip, a ship a-sailing, A-sailing on the sea, And it was deeply laden -with pretty things for me : There were raisins in the cabin, _ _ _ _
And almonds in the hold, The sails were made of satin, And the masts were made of gold. The four-and-twenty sailors

That stoOd between the decks, Were four-and-twenty white mice With rings about their necks; The captain was a duck, a duck, With a jacket on his back, . And when the fairy ship set sail The captain he said" Quack!"
THE WHALE'S REVENGE.

Not long ago eleven men belonging to a whaling ship were sent off in the small boat to pursue a whale that had been struck by a harpoon, off the coast of East Greenland. As almost always hap- pens in such cases, the wounded animal darted away at a great pace, dragging the boat rapidly through the water. Then, all of sudden, the .whale dived, or " sounded " as the " fisherman" say ; and, before the unfortunate men could cut the rope, the boat was hauled below the surface and the whole of the crew were drowned. This is one of the risks to which whalers are exposed, but the danger is so well known that it is strange the men were not prepared to meet it.

div.head: BRIGHT BOY.
div.p: A BRIGHT BOY.

A man thinks he has an exceedingly bright Office boy. A short time ago he posted in his shop win- dow a notice: "Boy wanted about fourteen years." A lad of that age, with little that was prepossess- ing in his appearance, came into the office and stated that he had read the notice. "Well, do you think you would like to have the place, my boy ? " asked the merchant, gazing patronizingly over the rims of his spectacles at the youth. "Yes," came the prompt answer. "I want the job, but I don't know that I can promise to keep it for the full fourteen years." Then the merchant remembered that he had left out a conima on his sign, but he told the boy he might have the place.

Authority is being given in the military commands at home for the furnishing of rooms in barracks which are to be devoted to the purposes of the Royal Army Temperance Association.

On Wednesday two schoolboys, James Fleming and Hugh Cairney, were walking along the railway close to the Stepps Station, near Glasgow, when they were overtaken by an express: Fleming was killed, and Cairney had one of his legs cut off, awl his arm and skull fractured.

div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
TAUGHT BY A PRINCE.

Many stories are related of the late Emperor Frederick of Germany, known to the people while he was Crown Prince as "Unser Fritz," .or "Our Fritz," which shows why he was so loved by his subjects. He was always kind to the poor, the sick, and the helpless, and one can easily understand how, during the war of 1870, the terrified French peasants so quickly learned to feel confidence in the commander of the invading army. One day while lie was Crown Prince he was paying his accustomed visit to the school at Born- - stedt, and talking to the children, when a telegram was handed in to the schoolmaster, informing him of the sudden and severe illness of his mother. "Go at once!" said the Prince, "and leave the school to me! " The schoolmaster at first hesitated, but was at, length persuaded to hurry off, and the Prince continued the instruction of the astonished but delighted scholars until late in the morning, when the clergyman arrived and relieved the Prince from his duties as schoolmaster.

DAYS OF BIRTH. Monday'rs child is fair of face, Tuesday's child is full of grace. Wednesday's child is full of woe, Thursday's child has far to go, Friday's child is loving and giving, Saturday's child works hard for its living. And a child that's born on the Sabbath day Is fair and wise, and good and gay,

WHERE THE BEAR IS A PET. Among the Ainu of Japan the bear is kept as a kind of pet. But for the fact that the. people do not pay rent, it might, like the Irishman's pig, bø describe as the " gintleman that pays the lint."' Brought to the hut as a cub, it is allowed the run of the wretched hovel until it has reached such a size that it becomes more than able to take care of itself. Then ailog cage is built for it, and there it is diligently fattened until the family can no longer resist the temptation of feast, when it is slain and eaten amidst great rejoicings, the skin being used either for clothing or as a blanket.

THE GOBBLER AND THE GANDER. Said a Gobbler to a Gander, with a proud disdain- ful glance, As they met one afternoon, in a farmer's yard by chance, "You're the most ungainly fowl that I meet throughout the day, As you waddie, waddle rouna in your slow, ungrace- ful way; And to tell the truth, my friend, if I looked as bad as you, I would seldom walk ahroad, but would hide my- self from view. Said the Gander to the Gobbler," Oh, you needn't swell with pride, Just because your legs are long and you spread your tail so wide, For in spite of all your airs, I am smarter still than you. I can swim, and I can dive, something you can never do." Then the Gobbler turned away, with a visage red as flame, In a stack of barley straw to conceal his head in shame.

div.head: NURSERY TRAGEDY.
div.p: A NURSERY TRAGEDY.
When the bough breaks the cradle will fall, Down will come baby, cradle, and all," sang little Lina, as she walked up and down the nursery with her doll in her arms.

"Let me have it," said her cousin Charlie, who was staying on a -visit with her, and who had become the tyrant of all the dolls and their little mistress as well, but Lina shook her head resolutely. "Oh, you selfish girl ! " said Charlie, and was beginning to tease, when nurse came in and stopyyd. him.

"o," she said, "of course you vill not have any more dolls, when you have spoilt four already this morning. lam going to take Miss Lina out for a walk, but you will have to stay in the • garden this morning because you have been naughty." 'Charlie was beginning to pout, when an idea struck him. Without a word he raced downstairs, and nurse dressed Lina, and went out. A few minutes after, he came creeping upstairs, took Lina's doll out of its cradle, and put it in the per- ambulator; he also wrapped a towel round Fido's head. Fido was a very dignified pug dog, and he did not like this at all, but Charlie took him up in spite of struggles and snaps, and thrust him in the perambulator too. " I will do what I like with Lina's dolls," he said. 4‘ 11l take this one for a walk." But the staircase ! Charlie, however, was not to be daunted. The perambulator was to go down- stairs! And down it did go aftet a minute or two with a will ; Fido, meanwhile, uttering howl after bowl, for his tail was getting unmercifully pinched, and Charlie sitting on the top stair looking help- lessly at it; then, lastly, the terrific crash when it came to the bottom! Poor Lina 1 She did not know how true those words would come when she sang-7_ -

document was under seal. He pointed out that that was puce nonsense as the only seal it was under was the seal of the Carporation, which made the contract binding. There wereactually Town CouncillorT,business men,who believed that the contract was nndera seal and could not be inspected. He therefore brought a resolution before the Council that he should have access to all papers and works in regard to the contract, and that was passed. He went to the Water Engineer and asked to see the contract, but he was informed that the Town Clerk had it. Accompanied by a fellow-Councillor he waited upon the Town Clerk but was refused permis- sion to see the contract. The members of the Council were supposed to be practically the managing directors of the waterworks but yet they could not have access to that document, even when the Council had passed such a resolution as he had mentioned. It only showed

THE STRENGTH OF OFFICIALISM in the town. He made the assertion that the contract would cost the ratepayers .250,000 instead of £24,000, but the chairman of the committee rose in the greatest indignation and said that was a deliberate lie. On an Investigation Committee being appointed it was found that the contract was over £55,000 then and ultimately the contractor sent in a claim with reservations for over £7n,000. Twelve months ago they were threatened in the Council that if they interfered in the matter the contractor would at once serve a writ upon the Corpor- ation and they would be subject to various pains and penalties. No writ had arrived yet ; but that incident shown how weak men in thecouncil could be frightened. He had found that in public life the greatest difficulty to light against was the ignorance of Town Councillors. (Hear, hear). They did not trouble to find out all the details and act on their own initiative. Very often a councillor did not know any more of the business of a committee than that audience did, but yet he would go to the Council meeting and vote for the passing of the minutes. What was required was A NEW MUNICIPAL CORPORATIONS ACT.

They had the District Councils, County Councils and Parish Councils Acts which provided that if those authorities spent money wrongfully the Local Govern- ment Board auditor could surcharge them the amount. There was ao surcharging a Town Council. (A Voice : "The sooner there is the better.") The Manchester City Council could spend £lOO,OOO and not be subject to surcharge. The Warrington Council passed a stand- ing order that no goods exceeding £2O in value should be bought without getting a public tender. In the electricity department 6,000 tons of coal was purchased without a tender and some of that coal was 3s. above the market price. He brought the matter forward and pointed out that it was against the standing order. The chairman of the committee, however, pointed out that it was a trial order—(laughter) —although it had been going on for two and a half years. Councillor Pemberton then referred to the building of a new school in which the tender accepted by the committee exceeded the specified amount of ten guineas per head. When he moved at the Council meeting that the matter be referred back he was defeated, the chairman of the committee stating that it was the best they could do. The Non-Traders, however,were determined to stop it and at the special meeting it was knocked on the head. New specifications were got out and this week a tender was accepted for £8,060 as compared with the originally accepted tender of £11,400. (Applause.) There ought to be Government control which would make it an easier matter to stop excesses. (Applause.) They could expose trading by limited companies or private firms, but they could not put their finger on ' commission. There shonld be Clerks of Works appointed by the Government, who would not "care a hang" for the Mayor. Aldermen or Councillors. He knew of a case not a hundred miles from Manchester where a Govern- ment undertaking was in progress at the same time as some Town Council work and materials identical with those which were refused on the Government work were accepted on the Town Council job. (Laughter.) Municipal accounts ought to be audited by the Govern- ment auditor. (Hear, hear). As to the saving of rates in Warrington, the greatest disappointment of the agita- tion was that owing to the education rate they did not appear to reap the advantages of their work. It was difficult to get the man in the street to appreciate the fact that they had saved hi= is. 10d. when he was only paying 4d. less. If he had his way he would not give any man a municipal vote unless he paid his rates direct. (Applause.) On one occasion he (Coun- cillor Pemberton) had to bring up a case with regard to the conduct of an official, but he was told it was out- rageous to do such a thing. They could understand a, new member being discouraged when, on bringing for- ward information, he was set upon by the Chairman and the old hands. If they wanted to alter that state of things they must arouse the interest of the ratepayers. As instancing how municipal undertakings were man- aged, the Water Committee which controlled such a huge capital, met fortnightly on an average for fifteen minutes. div.head: WORK OF THE NON-TRADERS.
div.p: THE WORK OF THE NON-TRADERS.
MR. DODDS AND COUN. PEMBERTON ADDRESS A MANCHESTER MEETING.
A New Law Wanted.

Mr. James Dodds and Councillor Pemberton spoke at a meeting held by the Manchester Ratepayers' Association in the Memorial Hall, Albert Square, on Monday evening to protest against "the Moloch of the rates." In view of several expensive schemes which are being brought forward by the City Council, considerable interest was taken in the proceedings and there was a large attendance. A large poster at the entrance of the hall proclaimed the fact that 11r. Dodds and Councillor Pemberton would "tell what Warrington ratepayers have done." The policy of the City Council came in for severe criticism at the hands of numerous speakers. Mr. James Saxon, who pre- sided, stated the position of the Association in a concise and telling manner. They were not, he said, necessarily hostile to the City Council. Their object was the economical and efficient administration of the city, and they would give the City Council their sup- port whenever it strove for this. They gave their support, for instance, to the Council in the endeavour to secure proper control over the expenditure of the various committees. A strong Finance Committee was needed, with power to revise or reject large financial schemes which did not meet proper require- ments. At present no such scheme was in operation, and until it was in satisfactory working they must continue their present campaL,cm. The Moloch of the rates had already swallowed up the reduction of the Ship Canal rate year by year. Yet they did not appear to be better off, and the committees of the Council were even now seeking powers to carry out expensive schemes which would send the rates still higher. Some of these he alluded to, such as the schemes for a new reference library, a new picture gallery, and a teachers' training college. A number of Manchester speakers followed, and strongly deprecated municipal extravagance. The Chairman then said there were some people who questioned the value of Ratepayers' Associations—who in fact, said there was no need for them. The members. however, believed such an association served a useful purpose and so did many of their Aldermen and Coun- cillors. They thought, however, that it would be wise to introduce to a Manchester audience gentlemen who could tell them how a Ratepayers' Association had benefited a neighbouring town and he bad pleasure in announcing that Mr. Dodds and Councillor Pemberton would tell them something of what had been accom- plished at Warrington.

- Mr. James Dodds expressed regret that as he was not in the best of health he would not be able to go into matters as fully as he would like. However, he had with him the best man they had in the Town Council and he would doubtless be able to give much interest- ing information. Their movement in Warrington had been the

div.head: GREATEST MORA L OvEM ENT
div.p: GREATEST MORA L OvEM ENT

which had been seen in the town for a generation, or, indeed, since the incorporation of the Borough. They began with a meeting something like the one he was now addressing, and it was crowded to the doors. A week later they had a meeting of 2,500 people in the largest hall in Warrington, with another 2,000 unable to gain admission, and he hoped that in a city like Man- chester they would have some such history a littlelater on. (Applause.) They found five years ago in Warring- ton that the great majority of members of the Council bad axes to grind. He did not know whether it would not be possible to count on the fingers of one band the men who were not getting something out of their positions as members of the• Council. There was a compact between the two political parties with regard to municipal elections, and this meant that the party compact leaders plus two or three of the chief officials settled the whole of the business-of the ratepayers in the Council. The bulk of the others were mere dummies or men who had been put there by those who led the two parties, and there were no contested elections for two or three years. The Non-Traders commenced their movement first of all because they found that the gentleman who was Mayor at that time was benefiting largely out of contracting with the Corporation, and so were many others. Within a few moapths prior to their com- mencing the agitation, something like

div.head: ELEVEN OR TWELVE LIMITED COMPANIES
div.p: ELEVEN OR TWELVE LIMITED COMPANIES

were started, chiefly composed of members of the Cor- poration, and formed for the purpose of doing business with the Corporation. There was a company for white- washing the Town Hall and that kind of thing— (laughter)—and that particular firm got three contracts for painting and decorating three of the principal municipal buildings. Immediately after the ft.,itation started, the head of the company paid out the Councillors who were members of it, because of the exposure, and paid them something like 50 per cent. premium with the share money they had invested, so that they did pretty well out of the business (Laughter.) Most of these companies had been driven nut of existence now, but there might be one or two left. Of course, the very big concern which caused them to commence the fight was still going on, but it was not doing anything like the same business with the Corporation and the head of it was not now a member. He (Mr. Dodds) was returned to the Council iy a very large majority in the cause of civic purity, although he did not canvass a single elector. Councillor Pemberton was also returned and the Non-Traders swept the board, getting some 3,200 votes against the combined 1900 of the Tory and Liberal parties. (Applause). The rates then were 7s. 10d. in the .C; now they were 7s. 6d. But when the agitation began there was no School Board in Warrington arid no education rate, whereas the rate for education now amounted to is. 6d. He therefore claimed that the work of their Association had really reduced the rates by is., 10d. (Applause). When he (Mr. Dodds) entered the Council the gentleman who bad been the Mayor and who had benefited so largely from trading with the Corporation resigned his seat, stating in his explanation to the Mayor that now that he (Mr. Dodds) had been returned for the Town Hall Ward it was a sign that he WAS not wanted and be would get out. (Laughter). Mr. Dodds then described. the circumstances which led to his resignation from -the Council, the er-member he bad referred to being nominated at a bye-election almost at the last moment but withdrawing when he (Mr. Dodds) came out in opposition to him. As he (Mr. Dodds) had previously promised to support the Labour candidate he then felt bound to withdraw from the field, and, he thought on the whole he was better outside the Council. When he was returned for Town Hall Ward, be was placed on the Finance Committee—in fact he, had all the best committees offered to him, perhaps owing to the big majorities behind the Non-Traders. The first day he attended a Finance Committee meeting he saw accounts passed which were not initialled by anyone. When he called attention to the fact. the Borough Treasurer said that at times they had to get accounts passed and cheques signed before they had been passed by the com- mittees which had ordered the goods. That was stopped from that day—(applanse)—the Mayor, Mr. J. Charlton Parr, who was an indepandent man,agreeing that it was entirely wrong. Then he came to an account in the name, as he conclnded, of a member of the Council but the Borough Treasurer assured him that it was the Councillor's son. That might seem a small matter but he wanted to know bow the Councillor could net straightforwardly and independently if he was told that his son would get no more orders if he did not Ivote in a certain way? A few weeks after the Non- Traders were returned, a. proposal was brought forward to

div.head: EXTEND THE WATERWORKS
div.p: EXTEND THE WATERWORKS

at a cost of £90,000. They made up their minds to tight that and on going into details found that great blunders had been made in working out the scheme. This became known to certain of the officials and as one result nothing more had been heard of the scheme. (Applause.) The extra water was not wanted for they had provision for ten million gallons more than they were using, without incurring aiditional heavy expenditure. Another scheme which the Non-Traders strongly opposed and which was defeated was for the expenditure of another £ll,OOO on the Technical school-15,000 for a staircase and the remainder for a hall for recreation, dances Br.c. (Laugh- ter.) Warrington owed more, in his opinion, to Coun- cillor Pemberton than they in Manchester owed to any man as a municipal reformer. •He had done a splendid work and was looked upon as

THE BEST MAN IN THE COUNCIL. Councillor Pemberton was determined to probe to the bottom of a waterworks contract, which was to have cost £24.000, and for which a bill had now been sent in amounting to .£76,000. He saw that there was some- thing wrong three or four years ago, and asked for tbe quantities and the contract. No one would let him see anything, both the Town Clerk and the Chairman of the Committee refusing. As a matter of fact not a member of the Water Committee had seen the contract under which so much money was boing spent. Mr. Dodds then referred to the difficulties which Councillor Pemberton had experienced, and to the allegations unsuccessfully brought against him. At one of their great public meetings held subsequently—the finest series of municipal meetings, he believed, ever held in this country or in the world—a vote of confidence in him was cordially passed. (Applause.) Councillor Pemberton said the Waterworks Contract question showed how the ratepayers' money was wasted and what little influence even members of the Council might have. He knew from outside information that the contract was going wrong, but unfortunately he was the only member of their party' on the Water Committee then and a lively time he bad of it. (Laughter.) First of all he moved that he should be allowed to inspect the contract to see if it was being properly carried out, but that permission was refused as, it was said; the

div.head: HELD RESPONSIBLE
div.p: HELD RESPONSIBLE

they would soon want to know more about things. There was too much officialism—red tape in the Governemt could not compare with it. Whatever mistakes a Corporation oqicial made the ratepayers had to pay for them. Tt was for the ratepayers to waken up and demand reforms. (Applause.)

div.head: MR. PIERPOINT'S PARLIAMENTARY REMINISCENCES.
div.p: MR. PIERPOINT'S PARLIAMENTARY REMINISCENCES.

Mr. ROBERT PIERPOTNT gave some interesting Parliamentary reminiscences in an address to the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society on Monday evening. He dealt with the life of an ordinary member which, he said, was not hard work but was an enormous tax on one's time. He (the speaker) had seen the sun rise on the terrace of the House; he had sat up all night, and had enjoyed himself; in fact, it surprised one how little it fatigued one to sit up all night. The House would accommodate not quite half the members. If it was an important night a member had to go early, and must be present at prayers to secure a seat. A card was put in the slit on the back of the seat, and one was supposed to remain in the House, hut, as a matter of fact, one went away. (Laughter). The most important debate he had ever attended was when the late Mr. Gladstone brought in the Home Rule Bill. Members stood outside—he did not mean in the open air,like one saw people waiting in a queue to go into a theatre—and the floor of the House, which was usually empty, was covered with chairs. He only got a place on a step in the gallery. Every place in the gallery was occupied. The House was big enough for ordinary purposes, because the great mass of the members did not bother themselves much by listening to every debate, and it was only on great occasions that any serious inconveni- ence was felt. There were, continued Mr. Pierpoint, members who never spoke, and never intended to speak. They were a useful category of men because if all the 670 members were speakers business would be impossible, not to speak of the strain which would fall on the Speaker. On the other hand, there were those who were always speaking. To the House they were a great nuisance; to themselves they were •ex- tremely profitable in some instances, because if they 'were young, and wanted to get into office, and had a fair amount of ability, to achieve the object in view there was nothing they could do better than to con- tinually inflict themselves on the House. (Laughter.) There was also the member who did not often speak, but when he did it was with solidity; to use the theatrical phrase, he was the " heavy father." Before addressing the House, one had to "catch the Speaker's eye," and Mr. Pierpoint caused some amusement by stating that on one occasion, when he wished to speaks he endeavoured to do so at 4.30 in the afternoon, but it was ten minutes to ten in the evening before he was called on, and he had then risen no fewer than 14 times. (Laughter.) His remarks were rapid, as they must necessarily have been in the circumstances. The House, on the whole; strongly objected to oratory. It did not like " high falutin," and, except from great men, it did not tolerate orations. It did netlike a man to show off. Of the orators he had heard he should place three as the best—the late Mr. Gladstone. Mr. David Plunkett, and Mr. John Redmond. One of the clearest speakers he had Japard was Sir Henry Fowler, and if he had to explain the principles of a Bill, one could be certain everything would be perfectly audible and perfectly clear. Mr. Balfour was one of the best speakers, and certainly far and away the most popular. even among the Irish Nationalists' over whom he held the rod. Mr. Balfour, however, had one fault, that of dropping his voice towards the end of a sentence. Sir Henry Campbell-Bannnerman was a good speaker, who used to prepare what he had to say, but, in his (Mr. Pierpoint's) bumble opinion, he did not trust himself enough. He spoke exceedingly well when be had to do so on the spur of the moment, but in a set debate, and when he knew the day before that he had to speak, he used half sheets of note paper, and went through the form of speaking, When,he was really reading most of what he said. The late Sir Wm. Harcourt did the same thing, but he was a better actor than the Premier. Reference was made to the committee work of the House, to the applications to members for seats in the Strangers' Gallery, to applications for loans of money —Mr. Pierpoint, on one occasion, !:aving been asked for a loan of ,£2.50 from a man whose only claim for assist- ance was that he bore the name of "Pierpoint." (Laughter.) Mr. A. J. JOLLEY proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Pierpoint. Mr. E. .1. HALT, in seconding, said he hoped Mr. Pierpoint would very often come amongst them, becaose he would find that, although a certain decision was made a little while ago, it was political and not per- sonal, and that his popularity in the hearts of thepeople of Warrington was as true as ever. (Applause.) The PRESIDENT (Alderman Bennett) said that long as the hours were in Parliament, Parliamentarians had a wonderful faculty for living to a great age. If one wanted to die early be must enter the Warrington Town Council. (Laughter.) It was lamentable to find that many who had tried to serve the town were only in office a comparatively short time, and yet how .few hours they sat at their meetings here, compared with the time spent in the sittings of the House of Commons The motion was heartily agreed to.

RUNCORN v. LEIGH: EXCITING GAME.

These teams met at Runcorn, before a fair attend- ance. In the opening stages Leah kicked across to Smith, who scored, Molyneux failing at goal. Play was hardly resumed before Leah and Smith went away with a dribble over the home line,the last-named player grounding the ball. Molyneux added a goal. Resum- ing, Jolley and Butterworth took play into the Leigh half, but a forward rush by the visitors enabled Nevill to follow up and , score after beating Harrison. Molyneux failed to improve. Deakin then kicked across to Hesketh, who got over after a short run, Jolley fail- ing at goal. Hesketh retired hurt, but came on again. Runcorn could not make headway, whilst the visitors kept up a strong attack, and before the interval Nevill added a further three points to Leigh after dribbling past Harrison. Molyneux failed with the goal kick. Half-time score :—Leigh 1 goal and 4 tries (14 points), [Runcorn 1 try (3 points). After the interval play was even for a short time. Johnson retired hurt, but resumed. A round of passing , between Jolley, Watton, Hesketh, Deakin, and Butterworth ended in the latter scoring a fine try at the corner, which Jolley failed to improve. The last- named player, however, made amends a moment later by placing a goal from a penalty kick. Flanagan then put in a short kick to the Leigh custodian, but Walker rushed up and snatched the ball from Clarkson's bands and grounded under the posts, Jolley adding a goal. [Jolley had an unsuccessful drop at goal, but Padbury shortly afterwards broke away and gave Runcorn the lead by scoring at the corner after a desperate effort. Jolley failed to augment. Near the close Jolley, Butter- worth, and Deakin gave a fine exhibition of passing, the latter scorinr, behind the posts for Jolley to add a goal. Resale': Runcorn 2 goals and 5 tries (21 points), Leigh 1 goal and 4 tries (14 points). Teams : Runcorn—Harrison, back ; Deakin, Butterworth, Hesketh, and Flanagan, three-quarter backs; Jolley and Watton, half backs ; Walker, Padbury, Leyland, Richardson Kennedy, and Dixon, forwards. Leigh—Clarkson, back; Smith, Johnson, Leah, and Nevill, three-quarter backs; Molyneux and Whittaker, half backs ; O'Neill, Lee, Webster, Gallop, Winstanley, aed Shaughnessy, forwards. Referee, Mr. H. Farrar, Keighley. Touch judges, Messrs. A. Jones, Warrington, and J. Edwards, St. Helens.
Friendly Matches. WARRINGTON "A" v. CADISHEAD AND IRLAM

There was a capital muster at the Wilderspool enclosure on Saturday to witness this match. The home side was strengthened by the inclusion of Fish, Tilley and Taylor, the first-named making his re-appearance since his accident incurred at Wigan in December. Following a lot of give-and-take play, Fish gave Fair- hurst a chance to open the scoring. Maintaining the pressure, Warrington had several penalties awarded, but all attempts at goal were failures, and it was not until near the interval that Knight scored from a forward rush. Warrington changing ends with six points to their credit. Turning round, Warrington immediately pressed and Kay landed a goal. Immediately afterwards Knight crossed, but by far the best try of the match was that scored by Roster, who, taking advantage of some loose play by the visiting backs, raced in from half-way. Jordan scored, after a long run, and near the close Fish made an opening for Jolley, this try being improved upon by Knight. Final result: Warrington,two goals six tries (22 points) ; Cadishead, nil.

div.head: MY DEAR NIECES AND NEPH
div.p: MY DEAR NIECES AND NEPH

.4 I suppose all of us, at one time or another, arc more or less ambitious; probably, there are some of my nephews whose aspirations reach as far as a motor-ear or a Lord phancellorship, and I should not be much surprised to know of many nieces who would not be against follow- ing the footsteps of Madame Patti. Now, I have no such gigantic dreams like these. There is about only one thing which would make me envious, and that is the Possession of beautiful piciures. I love to recall the happy times I have spent in strolling through the glorious Continental picture galleries, little dreaming of ever having a miniature one of my very own; and yet this week it is actually a realistic fact. Yes, I am the proud possessor of a picture gallery. My pictures are .not clothed in pic- turesque, golden frames, but I value them just: as much, and why? Because they are the gifts from my dear nieces and nephews. Of course, you all know now that I am referring to the Post Card Competition, for which I am offering a very nice prize to the sender of the best card. I must say that those I have already received are truly delightful, some of them little gems. All of my relations who have not yet sent one .will have the chance for another two weeks, after which the chance for the prize will be gone. I will now finish, with the best of good wishes, until next week.
UNCLE NED,

div.head: AN IMPOSSIBLE STORY,
div.p: AN IMPOSSIBLE STORY,

A certain king once made a proclamation that hc would give a golden ball to any tame of his tubjects who would tell him the most wonder- ful story, but; it, must be quite impossible for the story lb be true, or the prize would not be given. From all parts of the kingdom people came to him with remarkable stories; but the king declared that. tit was quite possible for one and all of them to be true, and the prkie was not awarded.' At last there came an old man, followed by two servants, bearing an immense jar between them. "May it please your Majesty," said the old your most excellent father borrowed from my father this jar full of gold, promising that your Majesty would pay the same amount back- to me." "Oh, that; is absurd and impossible!" said the astonished king, as he looked at the huge jar. "Then, if it is inapossible," said the old man, "1 have fairly won the golden ball; but, if my story be true, your Majesty ought to pay your _father's debt." Thus the laing was obliged to declare that the old man had won the prize.
