div.head: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
A 1,200-FOOT STEAMSHIP.

Mr. R. Oldham describes in Cassicr's 211aga- ei ne a monster transatlantic liner which, he pre- dicts, will be in existence within twenty-five years, and which will render travel by sea ab- solutely safe. This gigantic vessel is to be op: proximately 1,200 ft. long, 1251 t. broad, and 81ft. deep. with a draft of 40ft., a gross tonnage of 67,500 tons, a passenger capacity of 6,700 per- sons, engines of 170,000 horse-power, and a speed of thirty-five miles per hour. Built of nickel steel, with a strong protective deck, with twenty-four double transverse bulkheads uncon- nected by doors or openings, and with the bot- tom sheathed with coppered teak—such a ship, says Mr. Oldham, would be practically inde- structEble. Having before made successful pre- dictions of wonderful advances in naval con- struction, he regards this "coming ship" seri- ously, and not as a Jules Verne dream. The estimated cost is ihteresting—L3,4oo,ooo.

div.head: FERTILISING BACTERIA.
div.p: FERTILISING BACTERIA.

Professor Bottomley, in an interesting kcturo at Ipswich Social Settlement, disclosed some of the wonders of science as applied to the soil. The advantage of the four-course shift in far-i- -ing, he pointed put, was that the little nodules on the roots of leguminous plants. beans, peas. Sze.. are crowded with bacteria, the effect of which farmers found, by practical experience, was to enrich the soil for the next crop; but these, bacteria can be cultivated in the ,labora- tory and sent out in small packets to ittOculate the soil. Professor Bottomley held up a small package, not so big as an ordinary envelope, which, he stated, contained enough for two acres. He had, he said, sent out 100 samples from the laboratory at King's College, the cost of which was one penny each, eleaving out of account the cost of the laboratory equipment and staff. One Norfolk farmer, who used a sample, found, as a result of this "inoculation," that his peas were ready for picking three weeks earlier, and were 50 per cent. more prolific.

div.head: WILL THE SUN DIE OUT?
div.p: WILL THE SUN DIE OUT?

Professor T. J. J. See tells in the Munsey what the most , recent observations and 'discoveries have revealed as to the nature of the sun. On the question "Will the sun die out?" Professor See says: "Extending a theorum first derived by Ritter, I have proved that more than half of the sun's heat from the 1.);?!-rinning is still stored up in its flaming globe, and thus made available for radiation through future ages. This accumulated. beat, in connection with that yet to be produced by future contraction, assures us a future supply of energy three times as great as that required for the whole past activity of the sun. So far from approaching extinction, therefore, our sun is still in its youth, with the zenith of its glory far in the future. We need have no fear that it will soon die out and leave our world cold and wrapped in the darkrpss of everlasting night." The Professor adds that we "seem absolutely assured of a future duration of the sun for at least 30.000.000 years; and if the radia- tion be at a smaller rate it may amount to no less than 300,000.000 years"!

div.head: ARTIFICIAL SILK.
div.p: ARTIFICIAL SILK.

The manufacture of artificial silk from solu- tions of cellulose in cuprate of ammonia has so far been subject to a great drawback, says the Dyer. As is well known, the solution is forced through small holes into somewhat dilute sul- phuric acid. This coagulates the fine stream of solution into a thread, but. also injures the thread formed before it can be rinsed, especially when, as often happens, some of the acid gets entangled in cavities of the cellulose. Attempts have therefore been mad to use the coagulating acid in the form of vapour, in which state it does not injure the fibre in any way. Experi- ence has shown, however, that this method can- not be applied unless the ammonia has been pre- viously removed entirely, or for the most part. This is understandable, for a large volume of gas is easily saturated and rendered inactive by a small quantity of the liquid ammonia present in the cellulose solution. According to German patent 175,296. the ammonia can be removed from the cellulose solution in vacuo, without de- stroying the liquidity of the product, which can afterwards be forced through holes, and coagu- lated by hydrochloric acid vapour without under- going any loss.

div.head: GREAT COMET DUE IN 1910.
div.p: GREAT COMET DUE IN 1910.

The most famous of all comets, though not the largest and most brilliant, will be again visible in 1910, says Leslie's Weekly. This is Halley's comet, so called from its identification by the great astronomer who was the friend of Sir Isaac Newton. Halley's investigations of astronomical records led him to assert that the comet which he had observed in 1682 had appeared in 1531 and 1607, and to predict its reappearance in 1759. The fulfillment of his prophecy excited the most intense scientific interest and established beyond doubt the periodicity of comets and their move. ment in orbits determined by the law of gravita• tion. Its last appearance was in 1835, its period varying between seventy - five and seventy Nix years on .account of the perturbing attractions of Jupiter and Saturn in certain parts of the orbit. It, was by that time possible to calculate its movements with so much greater accuracy than before that it made its perihelion passage within four days of the predicted date. It was not then a very grand object to the naked eye, but the light of its nucleus surpassed that of second-mag- nitude stars and was comparable with that of some reddish stars of the first magnitude, such as Aldebaran and Antares. Its tail, while the comet was approaching the sun, attained to a length of 20deg.

div.head: SOUL OF MAN.
div.p: THE SOUL OF MAN.

Sir Oliver Lodge, in an address at White- field's Tabernacle, on "The Ascent and Fall of Man," said the question had been asked, "What is to be said of man's -higher faculties?" The answer to that which he proposed to make was, "The faculties and achievements of the highest among mankind in art, in science, in • philosophy, and in religion, are not explicable as the outcome of a struggle for existence. Something more than- mere life is possessed by us, Isomething re- presented by the words 'mind' and ' soul ' and 'spirit.' On the one side we are members of the animal kingdom. but on the other we are asso- ciates in a loftier type of cxistenco, and are linked with the Divine." Proceeding to deal with what differentiated man from the other forms of life, Sir Oliver said: " We are not only alive, we are conscious—that discriminates us from the vegetable world. It is only, the animal world that ,conscious of pain, and it is only the human part of the animal world that is self-con- scious, t. begins to discriminate between self and the eternal world. Our knowledge of our personal identity enables us to possess character and will and choice and freedom and all sorts of human attributes which • discriminate us entirely from the animal kingdom, and it is in this power of choice that we have risen to the knowledge of good and evil, and that wo have become truly Linked with the Divine."

div.head: WHERE EELS ARE BORN.
div.p: WHERE EELS ARE BORN.

A problem which for a long time has puzzled marine biologists is at length solved. It was not known whence came the thousands upon thou- sands of elvers which are found in rivers, streams, moats, Ponds, and ditches;. nor could there be discovered any difference to distinguish the male from the female. But now it has been established, by the energies of Danish marine investigators, working on behalf of the Interna- tional North Sea Fislicrins Investigation Board, that the elver is spawned of the Common eel at a depth of about 550 fathoms in the waters of the Atlantic, contiguous to the shores of the British Islands and South-Western Europe. From the eggs there appear larvte known as leptocephalus. transparent, jelly-like substances, .which in shape are flat and somewhat resemble the contour of a bloater without the tail, and With the head end more pointed. div.head: ANCIENT ORDER OF FORESTERS.
div.p: ANCIENT ORDER OF FORESTERS.
Annual Dinner

Court Warrington No. 430 held their annual dinner and social at the Blue Lion Hotel on Saturday, when the large Club Room was filled with members, who did justice to the good things provided by the host Mr. Lake. Afterwards the members were joined by con- siderable numbers for the smoking concert. The Chief Ranger of the Court No. 430 (Bro. Ernest Clavton),pre- sided and was supported by Bros. Peter -Peacock, ; Walter Smith, S.D.C.R. ; John Chrimes, P.D.C.R. and C.S.; George Maybury, P.D.C.R.; W. Hankinson, P.D.C.R. C.T. ; Trustees John Gregory and David Jones, P.C.Rs.; also Past Chiefs Will Payton, E. Roden, Joseph Massey, Will Taylor and others. Bro. E. CLAYTON, Chief Ranger, in his address heartily thanked the brethern present for theconfidence they had in him in making him their Chief Court Officer, and he hoped with the various Past Chiefs round him, that all the assistance and enthusiasm which they had would be centred around the Court he had the honour to preside over, to the increasing benefit.of the Order. (Applause.) The toast of "the King" was submitted from the chair, and drunk with musical honours, and it was mentioned that, as showing the great interest the King took in Friendly Societies, the Delegates at the Foresters High Court last August were specially invited to Sandringham to lunch, at which the Warrington District was represented by Bro. Peacock. (Applause.) Bro. PETER PEACOCx, P.D.C.R., proposed the "Order " and "Warrington District." He stated the longer he remained a member of this great Order, the more proud he became of it. He pointed out the membership of the Order at the end of last year was 919,713, and the funds amounted to £8,332,456, being an increase for the year of £302,268, although sick pay disbursed per member per annum averaged 14.62 days. He remarked that the democratic constitution of the Order was a guarantee of success, as the funds were controlled by the members for the members, and unnecessary expenditure was reduced to a minimum. Every member had equal opportunities of becoming the highest official of the Order, and he appealed to the members not to be content with the rapid strides the Ancient Order of Foresters was making,but to still push forward their endeavours with enthusiasm in order to do their.share towards reaching the million members. Regarding the Warrington District, he explained having just passed through the highest position, he was able to state that the united efforts of the members had been from every point satisfactory, and the unprecedented success obtained was such as to lead them on to still further and, better results. During the past year the district had paid out £238 funeral claims, £B9B for sick pay, and £44 to distressed members, but notwith- standing these disbursements the Warrington District and Courts were worth £6,s4s,being an increase of £306 for the year. The funds of Warrington District were well invested yielding 314 per cent. in Corporation Stocks, &c. He coupled with the toast the name of Bro. George Maybury P.D.C.R., one of the most respected officials in the District. (Applause.) Bro. GEORG MAYBURY in replying stated he had to respond on account of their District Socretary Bro. Davies being absent owing to his Court Meeting the same night. He explained he was not a member of the Court 430, but he always had the greatest pleasure in being amongst their members, whose fiery ambitions were so encouraging to the sister Courts. Even amongst each other there was a spirit of harmonious rivalry, and this an necessary,as the more enthusiastic the members were the better the results would be. During his 17 years as a Forester, he had watched the regular progiess made by Court 430, and be only, wished the others had made the, same headway. The ()Coors and members of No. 930 were an example to the District. He pointed out that the Ancient Order of Foresters had an income of £1,236,931, and an expendi- ture of £869,609 yearly and 200,000 members received relief last year. Such evidence showed what a power Friendly Societies must have in the country.(Applause)

div.head: PRESENTATION TO OFFICERS.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO OFFICERS.

- Four presentations were then made by Bros. W. Smith, S,D.C.R. ; J. Gregory and: D. Jones, Trustees,to Bros. W. Taylor, F. 0.8., framed eml4lem ; Bro. H. James, P.D.C.R., set of carvers ; Bro. J. Pidgeon,clock; Bro. T. Rhoden, P:C.R., Meerschaum pipe : for intro- ducing the most new members into Court 430, and they suitably replied, exhorting all members to go and do likewise during the year to still further the membership. Bro. G. M.kreurtY in submitting the toast of "Court Warrington No. 430," asked to be excused from any further lengthy remarks, although if he did say anything it was only deserved flattery to the members, and he trusted each one would only bring another addition to the ranks during the year. He would couple the name of Bro. John Chrimes, P.D.C.R., the able and esteemed Secretary, who, together with the other excellent officials, have made the Court what it is to-day. Bro. CIIRIMES, Court Secretary,in reply,stated he had referred back to the records of Court 430, and found in 1865 the membership was 70, and funds £66, whereas to-day there were 37-1 members with £1,509 at the back of them, whilst during the 42 years they had paid out £6,755 funeral claims and £1417 in sick pay. Coming, however, to the term of his secretaryship of 11 years, the Court had increased from 239 members and £1,071,t0 374 with £1,309 to-day. He thanked the members and officials very cordially for the assistance given to him, and he hoped those gatherings would, if possible,cement the good feelings of the members,and thereby strengthen the Court, whose steady prosperity should be the means of successfully competing against the Tontine Clubs which were scattered all over the town. (Applause). A capital musical programme was contribnted to by Bros. Joe Massey, Arthur Forster, Houghton, Hallwood, D. Jones, jun., Evans, Chattel! ; also the Co-operative Quarette, Messrs. C. and F. Fairhurst, Clayton and Wei r. Mr. Tongue was the pianist and the six hours spent werevoted to be the most pleasant evening the Foresters have had far some time.

The Mayor will then be requested to accept the memorial on behalf of the town. After his Worship's formal acceptance, a vote of thanks will be proposed to the General by Colonel F. A. Adams seconded by Colonel J. C. Ridgway. Following this the General will inspect the troops and the band will play the National Anthem. The ceremony over, General Buller will be escorted by the band snd the Ist V, B. Smith Lanca- shire Regiment along Bold-street, Sankey-street, and Bridge-street, on his way to High Legh. The statue is a very striking specimen of the Sculptor's art. It represents the late Colonel O'Leary, the respected head of the South Lancashire Regiment, as he appeared in the battle at Pieter's Hill where he fell whilst directing his troops. On the granite base of the memorial are three bronze panels, one bearing an inscription setting forth the fact that the memorial commemorates the men of the South Lancashire Regiment who fell in the South African campaign, another containing a list of the names of the soldiers, and the third recording the following engagements in which the regiment took part : —Spion Kop, Vaal Krantz, Clenso Kopjes, Tugela Heights, Pieter's Hill, Relief of Ladysmith, Bothas's Pass, Laing's Nek, Alleman's Nek, and the occupation of Wakkerstroon, Utrecht, Vryheid. On Friday evening the non-commissioned officers and men of the 2nd South Lancashire Regiment,along with representatives of the Militia, Ist and 2nd Volunteer Battalions, and the staff at the depot, will be entertained at dinner at the Parr Hall. It is also the intention to invite local veterans to take part in the festivities. A most enjoyable musical programme will afterwards be submitted. The bands of the 2nd South Lancashire Regiment and the Ist V.B. South Lancashire Regiment, pupils of People's College, and numerous local vocalists will take part. The public will be admitted to the galleries and seats may be booked at Bank House on and after Monday next. THE MAYOR'S REQUEST. In another column is published a request by the Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) that shop-keepers, employers of labour &c., will close their premises at noon in order that -all employees may have the opportunity of taking part in the celebrations.

The Finance Committee resolved that the tenders of the following firms be accepted, the contract in each case to remain in force for the twelve months com- mencing on the Ist April, 1907, viz. :—Mr. George Fern, brushes, &c.; Messrs. Dutton and Co.. pails, &c.; Mr. William Monks, soap, (tc.; Mr. J. H. Fleming, firewood and sawdust; Messrs. Peet and Hampson, window. oleaning ; the Warrington Corporation Gas Depark- meat, coke. It was also resolved, that the tender of Messrs. Thomas Locker and Co., Ltd., amounting to £8 55., for the supply of 30 wire waste-paper baskets for use in the school playgrounds, be accepted.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH AFFAIRS.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH AFFAIRS.
Meeting of the Parochial Committee.

The monthly meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee was held at the Hall Cafe on Tusday, Mr. George Pilling in the chair. Present :—Messrs. J. H. Clarke, T. Westbrook, H. J. Westbrook, W. Mclntyre, J. Hallows, J. W. Bouchier, T. Williams, J. Whitley, F. Pearson, and F. Warburton, 3. Swinton (surveyor) and George F. Ashton (clerk to the Runcorn Rural District Council). The Clerk said that in October last a letter was received from the Corporation stating that they would be prepared to extend their main to !Arab Brook if they could get MI extra consumption of gas from people en route, or, if not, the Corporation would be prepared to extend and charge an extra 21 per annum for a lamp until the consumption had increased on the main. It was decided to ask the Gas Committee of Corpora- tion to canvas the line of route asking for more con- sumers.

A letter was read from Mr. Albert Smith, Secretary of the Mersey Ports and Manchester District Confer- ence, Manchester stating that the railway companies had decided to extend the carriage boundary from the Ship Canal Swing Bridge along the direct road to London Bridge on the Warrington side of the Bridgewater Canal, including the business premises on both sides of the roads.

It Was decided to acknowledge the receipt of the letter, but expressing regret that there was to be no extension to Walton-road. The Clerk said at the request of Mr.- H. J. Westbrook he had prepared a list of attendances of the members during the last three years. There had been 42 meetings. The attendances were as follows :—Mr. Piling 3:3, Mr. Bouchier 32, Mr. Fairhurst 24. Mr. Mclntyre 28, Mr. J. Hallows 38, Mr. F. Warburton 31, Mr. J. H. Clarke 35, Mr. F. Pearson 37. Mr. .1. Whitley 3% Mr. H. J. West- brook 34, Mr. T. R. Westbrook 31, Mr. T. Williams 23, Mr. S. F. Welsby 27.

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith.

A Testimonial for the Infirmary. Sir,—Will you kindly allow me, through the medium of your valuable paper, to offer my testimony to the splendid services rendered to the patients treated in the Warrington Infirmary. The kindness and patience bestowed upon my little by boy, Arthur, after being operated upon a few weeks ego, was all that could be desired. I feel I cannot sufficiently express my thanks for all the help and sympathy shown to my wife and I, from th 3 Doctors downwards. If love. kindness and skill could have saved my dear boy I aii sure he would have been restored, as nothing seemed to be spared in order to bring relief and comfort. My wife joins heartily with me in this expression of sincere thanks. Yours truly,
J. 11. EDWARDS.
11, Garibaldi-street, Warrington, 14t11, February, 1907. •

div.head: BEAMONT SCHOOL.
div.p: BEAMONT SCHOOL.

On the recommendation of the Managers of the Beaniont Council school, it was resolved, that Mr. Edward W. A, Barber be appointed school-keeper upon the following terms, viz. :—(a) He to be paid a weekly wage of £2, together with an annual sum equivalent to the amount of the rates and taxes upon the school- keeper's house, and to be provided with fuel for his household use; (b) he to pay rent for the school-keeper's Amuse at the rate of ss. per week, and to bear the cost of lighting the same ; and (e) his engagement to com- mence on the 11th February,l9o7,and to be determinable by one week's notice on either side. Resolved, that arrangements be made for the insur- ance of the Beamont . Council school as foll3ws, —the buildings and school-keeper's house (separately) for a total sum of £12,000, and the furniture for a sum , of £1,500.

div.head: TENDER FOR COAL.
div.p: TENDER FOR COAL.

Resolved that, subject to a sample 'load proving satisfactory, the tender of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Ltd., for the supply of coal during the twelve months commencing on the Ist April, 1907, be accepted.
BE tMONT SCHOOL - STAFF.

The School Management Committee resolved that consent be given to the appointment of the under- mentioned teachers at the Beamont Council School, their engagements to commence on the date mentioned in each case, and to be determinable, in the case of the Head Teacher by three months' notice and in the cases of the assistant teachers by one month's notice, to expire on the last day of any calendar month, except the month of August : Boys' Mr. Donald Pine, Miss Fanny L. Hosier, Miss Ethel Yeomans, certificated assistants ' • Girls', Miss Ellen Shaw, Miss Annie T. Brodie, Miss Beatrice Wilcox,Miss Mabel England, Miss Lily Kirby, certificated assis- tants ; Infants, Miss Josephine E. Hetherington, Head Mistress (commencing salary £125, to be increased by £5 on April Ist) ; Miss Lucy M. Whittle, Miss Emily Bowles, cereificated assistants ; Miss Ada Buckley uncertificated assistant. RE-NAMING PEOPLE'S COLLEGE.

It was noted that the resolution of the Committee, in reference to the title of the Warrington British school, had not been approved and adopted by the Education Committee at their meeting on the 21st. January, 1907, and, after the communication which had been received from the Managers upon the subject had been .read and ,the matter further discussed, it was resolved, that it be suggested to the Board of Educa- tion that the Warrington British school be in future called the "Warrington Brewtnall school."

div.head: NOVEL SUGGESTION.
div.p: A NOVEL SUGGESTION.

A letter was read from the Superintendent of Instruc- tion in the Dayton public schools' Ohio, suggesting an inter-change of correspondence between scholars in that town and in this Borough, The suggestion was approved, and insiructions were given for the necessary arrangements to be made.

div.head: EMPIRE DAY.
div.p: EMPIRE DAY.

A communication was submitted from the Earl of Meath, calling attention to the desirability of" Empire Day" being celebrated by the school children in the Borough. It wis noted that that thy falls this year within the Whit-week holidiy, but it was resolved, (a) That the Managers and Head Teachers of the schools in the Borough be requested to see that appropriate reference is made in the schools to the occasion; and (b) that His Worship the Mayor be informed that the Committee will endeavour as far as possible, to fall in with any arrangements he may have in contemplation for celebrating the day, so far as it affects the school children.
SWINI NI ING INSTRUCT lON.

It was resolved that arrangements be made with Mr. G. A. Barlow, Superintendent of the Corporation Baths, to instruct the scholars from the public elementary schools in the Borough at the Baths in the art of swimming during the approiching season; he to be paid the sum of <£4o in respect thereof, the Committee also bearing the cost of the additional assistance, which will amount to about 10s. per week during the season.
FAIRFIELD SCHOOL

On the recommendation of the Sub-Committee appointed to consider the organisation of the Upper Girls' department of the Fairfield school, it was resolved that, subject to the Managers concurring, tha,Com- mittee will, on the retirement of the present Head Mistress, sanction the appointment of an assistant in charge at a salary in excess of that of the other assist- ants in the school, this appointment to terminate on or before December 31st, 1907; the whole question to be reconsidered and permanently settled in the meantime.

NONE BUT LOCAL HEAD TEACHERS? Considerable discussion took place upon the desir- ability or otherwise of giving instructions to the Managers of Council schoots when appointing Head Teachers to appoint only those who are employed in schools under the Committee, but no motion was taken in the matter.

SITES TO RE SECURED. At the meeting of the Sites and Buildings Committee, on the recommendation of the Sub-Committee appointed to make enquiries as to the land available in the neighbourhood of We!lfield-street on which to pro- vide a public elementary school, it was resolved, that the Board of Education be approached with a view to seeing whether, in the event of the committee succeed- ing in securing a plot of land adjoining the public park in that district, they would sanction the use of that park as providing the requisite playground accommoda- tion for the new school. Also, that, in view of the difficulty of obtaining sites, steps be at once taken to secure sites for schools in those parts of the town where they may be needed during the next few years.

div.head: BOLTON sciroor„
div.p: THE BOLTON sciroor„

It was resolved (a) that the tender of Mr. Harry Fairclough, amounting to £8,062, for the erection of the " Bolton "Council school, be accepted ; and (b) that application be made to the Local Government Board for their sanction to the raising of a loan to cover the cost of the erection and furnishing of the building.

THE CLERK OF WORKS. Resolved that Mr. Henry Hallard be appointed Clerk of Works for the" Bolton" Council school at a salary at the rate of .£3 per week; the engagement to com- mence from a time to be hereafter fixed, and to be determinable by one week's notice on either side.

• The Examiner, Saturday February 16 1907, NOTES ON GAMES AND OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. LANDLORDS AND THE NEW ACT.' ATHLETICS. Mr. King on Earl Egerton's Action. Mr. A. J. King, M.P., the representative of the Knuts- ford division, was interviewed in London on Wednesday RUGBY FOOTBALL,. by a correspondent of the "Manchester Evening News," and asked for his opinion upon the action of Earl Egerton of Tattoo, who, in anticipation of the new Agricultural Holdings Act coming into force, has given notice to his tenant farmers so that their agreements may be revised. ' I find," said Mr. King, "that Earl Egerton, though the most prominent, is not the only landlord who has taken advantage of the postponement until 1909 of the date on which the new Agricultural Holdings Act come into operation. I learn that such notices have been given in many other instances' and will probably be given in many more. No doubt the sole object in securing the postponement of the date was to get present tenancies terminated, if possible, so that before the New Act comes into operation the landlords could get new agreements. "The mere fact of a notice having been given is nothing unless some onerous conditions are put in the new agreement. If it be merely a matter of simplify- ing agreements there cannot be anything to be said. We always expected that the unscrupulous landlords would give notice to their tenants, but it may be that some will give notice without any serious intention to impose onerous terms in the new agreements." But suppose Lord Egerton, or any other landlord, does demand the imposition of such terms?" the interviewer asked. "In that case," replied Mr. King. " we shall have to secure a trade union of tenant farmers or something of the sort—a combination of tenants who will refuse to take land except on fair conditions. it will be impossible, of course, for the landlords, however unscrupulous they. may be, to contract out of the Act, but they may impose a higher rent, or they may do other things which will take away many of the advantages the Act was intended to confer on the tenant.' "What is the nature of those possible conditions other than increased rent ? " "Well, there may have been privileges in regard to game which may now be withdrawn. I understand from farmers that there are many conditions of that kind which leave the landlord plenty of scope for any action he desires to take. As it will be impossible for a landlord to get rid of a tenant on political grounds after the Act comes into force without paying him full compensation there may be an intentioa to get rid of obnoxious tenants now. As to Lord Egerton, we do not yet know what his intentions may be, awl must wait until we do know before we ran take any action."

The annual congregation gathering in connection with St. Peter's Church was held in the schoolroom, John- street, on Monday evening. From 200 to 300 parishion- ers and friends were present, the tables being presided over by a number of lady members of the congregation. After tea an entertainment was given, presided over by Mr. Joseph Bamforth, people's warden, who was supported by the Rev. B. Percival (vicar), the Rev. R. Russell (curate), Councillor Steel and Messrs. Joseph Taylor, P. Edgar, T. Reddish, J. Greaves, and J. 4. Hands. 4 The CHAIRMAN said the past year had brought its troubles as well as its joys. The position which he was holding that evening used to be taken by one who was far more fitted for it than himself. He referred to his past colleague, Alderman John Roberts. No words of his were needed to recall to their mind his devotion to St. Peter's and the noble work he did there and the very deep interest he took in their parish. (Hear, hear). With reference to other matters he was glad to say that .the church was going on well. They had much to be thankful for. The VICAR alluding to the education question said he was very pleased to know that for the present, at any rate, the difficulties had been overcome. He urged upon all present the importance of using their influence to prevent the Church schools being taken away from them. (Applause.) The musical part of the programme was of a very interesting character. Glees were given by the junior members of the choir. Master Jack Greaves' a member of the choir, sang two solos, and Miss Marie Houghton, of Daresbury, charmed the audience with her beautiful vocalization. The humorous element was in the hands of Mr. J. Hands jun., and left nothing to be desired. The tit-bit of the evening was supplied by a little boy, aged five years, named John Young, of Padgate, who gave two recitations in an admirable manner for one so young. He also delivered a stump speech in character, for which he was loudly applauded. The entertainment was called with a conjuring ,exhibition by Mr. Lloyd, who is entitled "The Young-Marvelle." On the motion of Councillor STEEL, seconded by the Rev. R. RUSSELL, a hearty vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman. The singers were also thanked for their services, on the motion of Mr. JOSEPH TAYLOR, seconded by Mr. T. REDDISH. St. John's Presbyterian Church. Annual Congregational Tea Meeting. On Thursday evening the annual tea meeting in con- nection with St. John's Presbyterian Church, Winwick- street, was held in the Church Schoolroom. An excellent tea was served to a gathering of about 100 members of the congregation and friends by the following ladies, viz :--Mesdames Butterfield, Brown, Ditchfleld, Jowett, Smith and Walker, and Miss Naylor. The chair was occupied by the Minister, the Rev. J. L. Milne, 8.D., who was accompanied on the platform by the Rev. C. L. Stowe Methodist Church, Legh-street, and Mr. R. Stowe, Treasurer, Manchester Presbytery. After tea Mr. Milne said he wished, briefly, to thank all those who had helped in the work of the church during the past year He hoped everyone remembered they were serving God. God acknowledged service. Let them strive to be faithful, and God would not forget. Every good work was difficult, and what work could equal that of God's Church ? He hoped that at the beginning of the New year they would all make good resolutions, and determine to keep them. He would not detain them longer, but wished all a happy evening.— During an interval in the programme a short address was delivered by Mr. R. Barclay. He thanked them for inviting him to the meeting. He was delighted to see so many young people present, so many young ladies and so many mothers, but sorry to see so few fathers. If their church was to prosper the ladies would have to work, and they wonld also have to make the men work. He had a strong feeling, a strong respect and a great sympathy for to !miles of their country—the more so as he grew older. The mothers must see to it that their sons and daughters were trained to become useful citizens of their country. They wanted men to come forward and show they had a love for their country and their God. It was sad to see so many men and women not caring, as it were, how the wind blew. The young men must come forward and help all they could in the church life of the country. Let them not think for one moment that they would reduce their pleasures by so doing; and they would not be worse citizens but better. No doubt there were difficulties, there was downright hard work to be done, butdon't let them be down-hearted (an expression they often heard) ; they would find they would have a great reward. If ever in their history they wanted good and true men and women it was at the present time.— Still later in the evening a most encouraging and interesting address was delivered by the Rev. C. L. Stowe.—An excellent programme had been arranged,and was carried out under the able superintendence of Mr. C. W. Jowett (church organist). Pianoforte solos were given by Miss Ashforth and Miss Maggie Brown,' and violin selections by Miss Wilson. The choir contributed a glee and a dialogue sketch, and Miss Dewar a humorous recital, while songs were renderedsby Miss A. Adams and Messrs Tynan, Moon and Hunter; and a duet by the Misses A. and M. Adams, all the singers being deservedly and heartily encored.—The meeting con- cluded with the passing of the usual votes of thanks and the singing of the Doxology. THE NEW STREET. The Purchase of Hewitt's Property.

Following the lines of recent years the Warrington Musical Society concluded its season's public work with a concert on Saturday evening the programme of which was sustained entirely by its own members. That the public likes the innovation is shown by the fact that there was a good attendance and that con- siderable enthusiasm was aroused in the course of the evening. Quite an array of names of members —mostly made familiar by their figuring as dramatis personae in pleasantly remembered light opera—were announced as principal vocalists, while in support of these, and under Mr. Crossley's bliton, were the society's chorus and orchestra, the latter— let it be proudly said—only very slightly supplemented on this occasion by professional help. The miserere , scene from "lE Trovatore" engaged two popular and well-known members —Mrs. Arthur Booth and Mr. J. Rabbitt —in a most pronounced success, the honours of which a capable men's chorus and a nicely subservient orchestra should be I remembered as entitled to share to some extent. The performance was in many respects highly meritorious, ' although in the chorus the marked individuality of one or two tenor voices had the necessity of using the organ detracted from a true sotto voce and dirge-like effect at the part preceding the duet. Mrs. Booth in the early portion of the " scene " interpreted the tender aria "Love, fly on rosy pinions " with the finished ease and grace of a true artist, and so pleased wero the audience with the way in which the whole of this picturesque excerpt was presented that its repetition was loudly demanded. Miss Alice Bridge, Miss Garnett Ball, Mr. S. Hassall and Mr. J. B. Poole were associated in what proved perhaps the best specimen of concerted singing the madrigal "Joy and sorrow" (Sullivan.)—in which a nice balance of the unaccompanied voices made possible the realiza- tion of a most praiseworthy ensemble. And but little removed from this number, in many points of excellence, was the sextet " Who that knows how I love you" in which 'Miss Marie Houghton, Miss E. Taylor, Mrs. 113nnan, Mr. Rabbitt, Mr. Fieldhouse and Mr Bibby took part, though here the complexity- of the composition made it difficult to divine the particular faults owing to which it fell short of an ideal rendering. But it is due to say that the piece was loudly encored by an audience who listened to it with marked and dis- criminating attention. The chorus had nothing to sing that was not well within its powers. The most important item was the dramatic scene " Liberty " in which Miss Marie froughton quite satisfactorily sang the solo part. This work and several ones of less importance —" The dance" (E/gar), " Hail ! bright abode" (Wagner), and "Now tramp" (Bishop) —have been heard on several previous occasions at these concerts and they must therefore be now fairly familiar to the society's patrons. The market-chorus from " Masaniello " and two part-songs from the pen of Sir C. V. Stanford complete the list of the choral contributions, and while more or less effective and laudable linterpretations lof all these compositions were given, it was undoubtedly in the two part-songs, (and especially in. "Oh, breathe not his name ") that the highest expres- sion of the capabilities of the choral members was reached. Curiously, enough the part-songs betrayed least of all the society's present weakness, the recurr- ence of which is so much to be deplored viz., the want of a proper proportion and balance amongst the various sections of the voices. Where, may we ask, is now the fine body of tenors and basses which proved so promising a feature of the chorus in the earlier concerts of this season ? The fact that the programme was unusually short makes one wonder why a few songs, by members who have proved themselves worthy the distinction, were not, for this reason and for the sake of variety, interspersed amongst the mass of concerted vocal music to which reference has been made. Of the orchestral numbers and of the playing of the parts to the various choral items we can unhesitatingly speak in high praise, and, in congratulating the society on its evidenced all-sufficiency in attracting public support, special mention is due of its preserv: strong body of efficient instrumentalists. The" Rural scenes" suite, the" lolanthe " selection, and the" Cavalliera Rusticana " intermezzo, were all well played and deservedly applauded.

Tuesday was the day for the important match at Halifax, and as the thaw cantinued these was no fear of a hard ground this time. The morning broke sleety and wet, but that was merely an unpleasant detail, and both players and supporters departed at 10.40 for the hilly town. They got no further than Manchester luckily, where a telegram from Halifax intercepted them. Instead of frost it was snow this time, and six inches of it by noon proved too much for the Hanson Lane officials to . cope with. Whln the next away fixture is arranged I expect there will be an earthquake and the goal-posts will slip down a crack, or some such unlooked for mishap to prevent play.

Most of the Clubs managed to bring their matches off on Saturday, and one of the most interesting was that between Runcorn and Leigh. The Mather-Loners created a sensation by running up 14 points to 3, in the first half. It certainly looked as if they were g)ing to do Warrington a good turn in the South-West Lancashire Competition, but they flattered only to deceive. Runcorn were irresistible in the second half and scored 18 points while Leigh looked on. There is no doubt the Cheshire team are a very smart lot this season and it will be a battle royal on March 23rd, when Warrington attempt to rob the Linnets' nest.

. Warrington "A" team managed to play their match with Cadishead on Saturday, and a gool crowd turned no to witness the efforts of such exponents as Tilley, Taylor, Fish and Burgess. The latter was on the visiting side and generally off-side as well. Cadis- head were well beaten, of course, but the match has no bearing on the Combination Championship. Fish's appearance was a surprise in more senses than one. He had not been chosen to play and got a fine recep- tion, but his outline was truly aldermanic. j " Jack ' will have to do some hard training before luei is fit for League football, and I hope he will lose no time. about it.

Warrington still occupy the fourth place in the League and they should make the position more secure at the expense of Oldham to-day. The latter lost at Hull against the lovers last Saturday, and as Warrington owe them a drubbing they will probably lose again at Wilderspool. The homesters will have one of the strongest sides they have puts'in the field for some months. Taylor being fit again takes the place of Hockenhall on the wing, so that the three- quarter line will be exceptionally strong. Fish and Preston—the captain and sub-captain of the team—are both dropped for want of condition. The selected side is: Berry, full back ; Taylor, Isherwood, Dickenson, and Brooks, threequarters : Lees and Jenkins, half backs; Boardman, Thomas, Heath, Harmer, Naylor, and Shugars, forwards. The Oldham team will be : —Thomas, dash, " Birdie" Dixon, W. Dixon, Tyson, Lees, Yewlett, Ferguson, Avery, Smith, Longworth, Vowles,Topham.
The "A " team will also be strongly represented for the Combiroation match t-1 Oldham. Team :

Tilley, full-back ; Jordan, Jones, Cartwright and Knight, threequarters ; llockenhall and Kay, half- backs ; Jolley, Bradshaw,•Holbrook, Forster, Hewitt and Belton, forwards. Next Saturday there is at vacant date, and the " A " team will probably enter- tain a team picked from the Manchester and District League. Lambert is expected to re-appear in this match.

div.p: Ensuing Year.

Another increase in the rate for education purposes is involved in the estimates of receipts and expenditure which will be submitted for the approval of the Warrington Education Committee on Monday evening.; The total estimated deficiency to be made up from the rates is £16,671 134. 4d., as against £14,732 19s. 4d. for the year 1906-7. This means that the call upon the rates for education purposes will be about Is. 41d. in the £ as compared with is. 3d. for the year just closed. The following is a summary of the estimates: Committee. Expenditure. Receipts. Deficiency. s. d. £ s. d. s. d. School Attendance 1410 6 0 91 3 0 1319 3 0 School Man'g'inent 35684 3 0 29377 0 0 5807 3 0 I Sites and Buildings 385 0 0 25 0 0 360 0 9 1 Finance 9328 7 4 143 0 0 9135 7 4

There are no very striking features about I the estimates. The, increased deficiency is more ! than accounted for by advances of salary to teachers and officials, so that in other departments there must be a decreased expenditure. The salaries of teachers in the elementary schools are estimated to total £28,341 Bs. as against £27,222 19s. Bd. and under this head the opening of the Beamont school will make an increased demand upon the rates as the payment of salaries to the staff will very shortly come into operation. It will, we understand, be six or seven years before the ratepayers can expect any relief in regard to the salaries !paid to teachers as, of course, the annual increases take place in accordance with the committee's scale. The total expenditure on elementary education is estimated at £30,665 Bs. as against £20,589 16s. 4d. On the receipts side, grants are expected to produce £24,530; fees £1,691 and sale of books and materials £109; leaving a defici- ency of £4,335 Bs. On higher education the jexpenditure in salaries is estimated at £3,808 15s. as against £3,542 13s. The total expenditure in this department is anticipated to amount to £5,018 15s. and after deducting grants, fees and other sources of income, there is a deficiency of £1,471 15s. as com- pared with £1,300 13s. With regard to the Finance Committee's requirements, officers' salaries are put down at £,1486 as against £1398 10s. and school- keepers' salaries at £1,826 6s. as against £1,770 15s. Interest and instalments on Technical Institute loans are estimated to total £1,024 2s. 3d. as against 1,991 Ills. 10d., and interests and instalments on loans for Ithe new sehools (land and huildings) £1,568 9s. id. •as against £1,389 ss. 9d. The School Attendance Committee requires £541 18s. for officers' salaries as against £514 16s. fid. The maintenance of children in various institutions is estimated to cost £740 3s. as compared with £6BO ss.

div.head: WARRINGTON TRADES COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TRADES COUNCIL.
Criticism of the Labour Bureau.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council was held in the Bold-street Schools on Tnesday evening, Mr. T. Plumb presiding over a small attendance of delegates. MR. A. H. CROSFIELD, M.P., AND HOUSING REFORM. Mr. E. PLINSTOST, secretary of the Council, reported that he had communicated with Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M,P., asking him to assist the Government in giving effect in 1907, to the recommendations of the Select Committee on Housing Reform. Mr. Crosfield had written in reply, " I wish to thank the members of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council for the courteoes and encouraging nature of their communication. I have not by me here the details of the proposals but on your recommendation I can assure you they shall have my closest and most careful attention. I think, from the many speeches I have made in Warrington you and your friends will realize that lam not sanguine of any real and lasting solution of the housing problem until we have thoroughly dealt with the question of the taxation of site values. To my mind these vital problems are obviously and inevitably bound up together." The letter was received without comment. THE LABOUR BUREAU. The SECRETARY of the Warrington Branch of the' Amalgamated Union of Carpenters and Joiners wrote: "I am instructed by the members of the above Branch to inform the Trades Council of the methods that are being carried on at the Labour Bureau in dealing with applications for work. A short time ago the billowing notice was fixed in the window at the bureau: Several reliable joiners wanted.' Members of the above Branch, seeing it, made enquiries at the office and on replying to the clerk in charge that they were trade unionists all information was refused to them. The firm requiring men was found to be a wrong one and that they offered 255. a week instead of 425. We consider that if this is what the bureau is for the sooner it is closed the better." Mr. GREALEY thought something ought to be done. The office was maintained out of the rates and union men should have all information. It was not the time for them to be chicken-hearted. If the office was to be, ' used for the purpose of getting non-society men whilst trade unionists were out of work it wanted blowing up. Mr. RANDLES did not agree with the closing of the bureau. What he wanted was to stop firms trying to pauperise labour through the bureau. Mr. GREALEY 1 The clerk is a public servant who is working for cue section only. The CHAIRMAN said the whole affair was most unfortunate and it appeared to him that the sooner the office was wiped out of existence altogether the better. Mr. HALEY said that when they considered the ques- tion they must remember that the Uncmployed Bill— passed by a Conservative Government—was absolutely worthless, and they only accepted it as the foundation of a larger and more equitable measure. He could assure them that if they sent a resolution to the Distress Committee calling for the closing of the bureau, they would have a very large measure of sup- port. He must, however, warn them against that course. If they closed the bureau, and then, when they had a workable Bill, desired to re-open it, the people who assisted in its being closed would oppose them. Under the Act they could not exclude any employer or workman.
A. JOINER'S DELEGATE: Why should the men be asked whether they are union men and then refused information? Mr. HALEY: Mr. Fargher did not refuse tho information.
A JOINER'S DELEGATE : When the men said they were union men Mr. Fargher said "the job is no use to
Mr. HALEY: He .knew it was no use union men applying and therefore told them the job was no use to them.
Mr. MOORFIELD moved that a letter of protest be- sent to the Committee.
Mr. GREALER : Can an employer state whether he requires union men or not?

kr. HALEY: He can please himself. Mr. HICKENBOTTOM : We are paying out of the rates to support a bureau which helps to keep open "knob stick "shops. • Mr. PODMORE urged that they should distinguish between the methods and the institution. Mr. MOORFIELD : My idea is to send a resolution protesting against the methods employed in this parti- cular case.

Mr. RUSHTON said be was not disposed to condemn Mr. Fargber's methods. He took it that Mr. Fargher told union men the job was no use to them in order to save them a journey. Mr. PLINSTON thought Mr. Fargher did not deserve condemnation but that the blame rested upon the institution which, at present, was a complete farce and utterly opposed to right in regard to labour matters. He did not think he would mourn if the bureau collapsed immediately: Mr. PODMORE said that when they looked at Mr. Fargher's past it was not possible for them to suppose that he would do anything to injure trade unions. Mr. HALEY said the Distress Committee would give firms to understand that they could not allow the bureau to be used for the purpose of " knobsticking " labour. -
_ After further discussion it was decided taadjourn the question for a month.

Southampton Town Council on Wednesday confirmed the recommendations of the Estates Committee whereby the South-Western Railway Company will acquire 31 acres of submerged land in connection with their dock extension scheme on terms involving a money payment of $.500, and an undertaking, on behalf of the company, to reclaim 6 acres of mudland on the western shore.

STOCKTON HEATH. BENEFIT CONCERT.—Success attended a concert in aid of Mr. J. Bostock, of Stretton, which was held in the Institute, Stockton Heath, on Saturday evening. The Warrington Hormonic Choir gave admirable render- ings of " Comrades in arms" and " In absence';" while Miss L. Snelling sang with effect, "Come back to Erin" .and" A dream of Paradise." The Warrington concertina quartette treated the audience to several selections. Mr. G. H. Bennett ably sang " Anchored " and "The ont- post's vigil," whilst Mr. G. Gough pleased the audience with his illustrated song 'Asleep in the deep." Mr. J Hannan sang "Good Company" and, with Mrs. A. Parkinson, gave a good rendering of the duet" The keys of Heaven.' Mrs. Parkinson also sang" Down the vale" (illustrated) and" Awake." During the interval selec- tions from the " Messiah " were given on the grams- Phone by Mr. T. Williams. A selection of living pictures was supplied by Mr. William Parkinson entitled ' Grandpa and the butterfly" and casued much amuse- Ment. The humorist was Mr. J. Isherwood who kept the audience in roars of laughter with his humorous Bongs and received several encores. The accompanist W 8 Mr. A. E. Trow. The concert had been arranged bY Mr. Whitney, Warrington.
